description: The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) builds on the work of the Sustainable Intensification Innovation Lab (SIIL) Project in Bangladesh through the International Rice Research Institute. Their joint efforts aim to implement a transformative project in the polder zone, targeting the untapped agricultural production potential of the region. Since waterlogging is the main constraint for wide-scale adoption of improved production systems, the project implemented innovative catchment-level water and crop management for sustainable farming in the polders of coastal Bangladesh. Currently, the rice-sunflower production system is being introduced. The farmers cultivated HYV rice in the wet season that almost doubled the productivity. While sunflower was mostly cultivated under semi-mechanized practices that provides livelihood and income generating opportunities to farmers where most fields remain fallow in the dry season. The system productivity of rice-sunflower (10.3-14.1 t/ha/yr) increased by 2-3 folds over farmers’ practice and has potential to reduce edible oil import.
title: Diversified and intensified farming through rice-sunflower production systems in the coastal zones of Bangladesh

description: GROWSMART is a package of data science-driven advisories, developed using crop models and machine learning techniques based on historical weather and soybean yield data from short, medium and long duration varieties in the Chinyanja Triangle (consisting of regions of Zambia, Malawi, and Mozambique). Actionable farmer management options were developed in English and Chinyanja based on this analysis and shared with national governmental and non-governmental partners via GROWSMART.

description: This innovation describes the implementation of the sires’ certification in the framework of Community-Based Breeding Programs of small ruminants in Ethiopia. The sire certification system is described and areas that need to be strengthened are suggested. Currently, the existing certification scheme is based on the genetic worth (Estimated breeding value-EBV) of the sire and other technical requirements for certification including physical examination, semen assessment, mating ability and vaccination against prevalent infectious diseases. The innovation describes the institutional set up whereby the innovations is owned by the national system.
title: Improved access to certified sires from the Community-Based Breeding Program by smallholder sheep and goat farmers in Ethiopia and Mali

description: Orange-Fleshed Sweetpotato (OFSP) puree is a semi-processed product made by steaming and mashing OFSP roots. It is highly valued for its nutritional content, particularly its rich supply of beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A, which addresses Vitamin A deficiencies in populations at risk. It is used as an ingredient in various food preparations. OFSP puree is versatile and can be used as an ingredient in various food products, i.e. in Baking: bread, buns, mandazi, cakes, baby foods. OFSP puree derived porridge is used in the households and school feeding program.

description: To provide agro-advisory on a weekly and monthly basis to fishers in Myanmar, the Alliance partnered with the Village Link Company Limited to pilot the innovation and reach initial number of farmers. The advisories are based on seasonal and monthly weather forecast with the support of crop decision trees (CDTs) developed by the Alliance. Village Link provides advisories through their digital platforms such as the HTwet Toe application. It is now being piloted in select township in Myanmar. It is envisioned that after succesful piloting, with evidence of reduce agricultural and climate risks, the advisories will be tied up to financing mechanisms to improve access of fishers to production capital through loans.

description: This innovation develops an analytical approach for researchers to pair quantitative and qualitative research in multiple countries, to assess how social protection shapes the gendered impacts of climate change. The quantitative approach entails merging household survey data from randomized controlled trials on social protection interventions with weather data from satellite data or remote sensing. Doing so allows estimating the effects of climate hazards on gendered outcomes, and assessing how those effects change when climate hazards overlap with receipt of social protection. The complementary qualitative approach entails interviewing women and men in the same setting on how they perceive climate change and social protection’s role in helping them adapt, and what changes to social protection could better support them. The combined approach allows researchers to assess what impacts social protection has on gendered impacts of climate change, how and why patterns vary by context, and how to better design social protection.
title: Analytical approach for researchers to conduct mixed-method multi-country assessment of how social protection shapes gendered impacts of climate change

description: This sustainable land management (SLM) innovation draws on qualitative formative research, co-design of an innovation with partners, a quantitative impact evaluation testing the innovation, and resulting guidance for partners on implementing the innovation. This project is delivered as part of a multifaceted graduation model social protection program, SPIR II (Strengthen Productive Safety Net Program Institutions and Resilience II) that seeks to further sustain nutrition security and reduce risks to livelihoods for households participating in the Ethiopia’s national safety program, the Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), which provides consumption support in the form of cash and food transfers. The goal of the SLM innovation being tested is to leverage social protection to promote women’s engagement in sustainable land management practices. Strengthening women’s involvement in sustainable land management is seen as potentially important given that extreme weather events pose risks for poor households in rural Ethiopia and women may be disproportionately at risk from these shocks. For example, Kato et al (2021) find that plots controlled by women in Ethiopia are more prone to soil erosion and of poorer quality in terms of soil depth, and women’s participation in watershed committees is low. The sustainable land management practices being introduced may help protect women and their families from these shocks over the longer term as well as introduce an additional livelihoods avenue. The innovation tested includes providing training (to either women only or to both men and women from same households) and free inputs (tree seedlings, vegetable seeds and tools for home gardening) among participants of the PSNP public works program, thus helping to address constraints to accessing information and inputs, and assessing whether spousal cooperation is important for successful adoption of these technologies.
title: Design innovations in leveraging social protection for women's engagement in sustainable land management practices

description: The International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) and the Ethiopian national research systems have succeeded to work together to introduce community-based breeding programs and improved fattening technologies that are suitable to various production systems. At the same time, significant commercial and market-oriented patterns and practices are now emerging as result of the support. There exists some scientific evidence for the demand for livestock market facilities being developed and make them accessible, sustainable and guide a national effort. Along with these, ICARDA is collaborating with a private livestock marketing enterprise (Yazerber) to organize and launch a trustful and contented market linkages between sheep and goats producers and domestic consumers in and around Addis Ababa city. This activity is expected to increase sales of animals from target areas through increased market access and improves efficiency in well-organized livestock markets. Buyers have the option of buying their animals digitally.

description: The innovation is a bundle of three technologies for intensification of maize-small ruminants farming system in northern Ghana. The basal NPK fertilizer timing focuses on applying the fertilizer at planting stage of maize to reduce nutrient stress especially during the emergence-vegetative stage, enhance nutrient use efficiency and yield. Intercropping of cowpea at one week after planting of maize as a living mulch provides soil surface cover, increases soil moisture retention, adds nutrients through biological nitrogen fixation, suppresses weeds growth, and increases yield and food diversity. Harvesting of maize leaves below the cob leaf at silking stage (Leaf stripping) offers quality forage for livestock without compromising grain yield. The stripped maize leaf forage has a 40% higher crude protein content than the crude protein content of feed required for the body maintenance of livestock. Feeding strip maize leaf to small ruminants increases live body, slaughter, and carcass weights.

description: This innovation addresses the challenge of low grain yield and fodder availability in groundnut-small ruminant farming system in northern Ghana. Traditionally, smallholder farmers plant groundnut at a density of less than 10 plants/square meter. Planting ground at a density of 22 plants per square meter increases the rate of canopy closure over the soil surface which protects the soil from erosion, improves water infiltration as well as soil moisture retention, increases grain and fodder yields. The plant density of 22 plants per square meter can be achieved by either sowing the groundnut seed at a spacing of 30 cm inter-row × 15 cm intra-row or 40 cm inter-row × 10 cm intra-row. Feeding groundnut fodder generated from the 22 plants per square meter to sheep increases dry matter digestibility, live weight gain and nitrogen concentration of manure relative to feeding those generated from the farmer practice.
title: Optimal groundnut plant density for improved grain yield, fodder availability and quality in smallholder farming systems of northern Ghana

description: The EzyAgric is an App accessible on the Google Play Store, bundling various digital services targeting farmers and agri-input merchants. The services include Farm Manager for undertaking a Cost Benefit Analysis, and proper record management is accessed; Agri-shop, where a platform to digitally purchase genuinely affordable price agri-inputs from certified bulk agro-input manufacturers while providing an end-to-end feedback loop and a traceability trail; EzyCredits where farmers receive credits calculated based on the records generated from Farm Manager and Agrishop transactions as collateral, redeemable for purchase exclusively via the Agri-shop; Agri-Extension provides on-demand information and training tailored to specific agronomic needs. The Produce Market links farmers to aggregation centers established around off-takers and payments made directly to the farmer’s phone. A toll-free call and SMS platform is provided where non-smartphone farmers can access the services. The working model integrates women and youth with smartphones as community agents/service providers.
title: The EzyAgric app, designed by CIAT, provides smallholder farmers with an integrated service platform to support farm management and good agricultural practices, and access to agri-inputs and credit in Uganda.

The services include Farm Manager for undertaking a Cost Benefit Analysis, and proper record management is accessed; Agri-shop, where a platform to digitally purchase genuinely affordable price agri-inputs from certified bulk agro-input manufacturers while providing an end-to-end feedback loop and a traceability trail; EzyCredits where farmers receive credits calculated based on the records generated from Farm Manager and Agrishop transactions as collateral, redeemable for purchase exclusively via the Agri-shop; Agri-Extension provides on-demand information and training tailored to specific agronomic needs. The Produce Market links farmers to aggregation centers established around off-takers and payments made directly to the farmer’s phone. A toll-free call and SMS platform is provided where non-smartphone farmers can access the services. The working model integrates women and youth with smartphones as community agents/service providers. The EzyAgric app, designed by CIAT, provides smallholder farmers with an integrated service platform to support farm management and good agricultural practices, and access to agri-inputs and credit in Uganda.

description: Extension and sensitization campaigns targeting smallholder dairy farmers generally focus on milk sanitation, highlighting the importance of washing udders and using clean and appropriate receptacles such as steel buckets and milk churns. Processors indicate that milk sanitation is fine, but the quality of milk in terms of composition (butter fat content and solid non-fats such as proteins, carbohydrates, and minerals) often needs improvement. We pilot a short, engaging video that explains various strategies that smallholder dairy farmers can use to increase the compositional quality of milk, such as choice of animal breed, pasture management, and supplementary feeding. By better aligning the quality demands of processors with the supply of raw milk, processors can produce more at a lower cost, and these rents can then be redistributed throughout the value chain.

description: Two main innovations are improved seed varieties and the extension approach of the East West Seeds - Knowledge Transfer (EWS-KT) . The improved vegetable seed varieties result from advanced breeding techniques by East-West Seed with enhanced traits like yield, disease resistance, and adaptability to diverse conditions. Improved vegetable seed varieties empower smallholder farmers' production capacity, increasing productivity while conserving resources. This ensures that agriculture remains at the forefront of sustainable development and food security. The extension approach provides timely, accessible, and tailored information to smallholder farmers via EWS-KT’s extension agents, enhancing their decision-making and crop management. It also encompasses the innovative approaches of publicly certifying trained farmers – to increase innovation diffusion and product value – and educating smallholder farming households to optimize income use through an inclusive decision-making process. These innovative approaches hope to empower farmers with actionable knowledge for sustainable farming that can better their livelihoods.

description: A novel service for smallholder farmers consisting of quick, on-farm bean grain quality testing with low-cost, mobile test kits operated by local technicians from farmer organizations. Currently, grain testing is done centrally at the association's warehouse or processing facility, and this process needs to be clarified for the farmers. To make the quality-testing process more transparent and create awareness of bean quality and price determination, we will perform at-farm (on-site, with the farmer) bean grain quality testing focusing on the top three quality parameters typically evaluated later at the processing facility. Local technicians from the associations will be trained and perform the test on-farm. They will register the test results using an electronic form automatically delivered to CIAT and the Associations and leave a printed copy to farmers. Farmers will be more knowledgeable about the bean quality they can sell.

Clustering shrimp farming for traceability and certification strengthens backward linkages with farmers via aggregation, disintermediation, technology transfer, and enabling certification. _x000D_
In ACI (Advanced Chemical Industries) Agrolink, clustering shrimp farming organizes groups of 20-25 farmers with contiguous ponds into a cluster with direct shrimp procurement to process by the company. In BSFF (Bangladesh Shrimp and Fish Foundation), shrimp farmers commit to monoculture and are provided SPF-PL (Specific Pathogen Free Post-Larvae), cluster-level credit from designated banks, and a buyback arranged with specific processing firms. description: Growth, egg production performance and economic feasibility will be evaluated for candidate breeds (strains) across different agroecologies. Brooded and vaccinated chicks (28 to 56 days-of-age depending on the country) will be issued to on-farm households the three agroecologies. The male chickens will be evaluated on body weight until 20 weeks-of-age, while the females will be evaluated on body weight and egg productivity until 72 weeks. The test will be integrated with promotion of access to inputs and support services (feeds, flock health, training, markets).  The strains will be tested at three different flock levels (with a  household receiving 25, 50 or 75 birds of a randomly assigned strain). This arrangement will allow development of viable business models that consider productivity levels, contribution to livelihoods (income, women empowerment, and nutrition), techincal feasibility and sustainability of impact.

description: This product provides finance for cattle fattening through a profit-sharing model. Eligible smallholder farmers receive cows purchased by the company and then sell them back to the company at a guaranteed price or at a higher price they find in the market. Farmers keep 2/3 of the difference between the purchase and sale price, and the company keeps 1/3. This intervention is bundled with insurance to protect the farmer against cow death. Other possible services include subsidized high-quality feed and growth monitoring to increase the value of the cow. Women will be specifically targeted for contracts to increase their empowerment in a sphere where they are responsible for physical labor.

description: Risk-contingent credit (RCC) is a linked financial product that embeds within its structure an insurance protection which, when triggered, offsets loan payments due to the lender. RCC mitigates drought-related agricultural risks and provides access to credit for smallholder farmers, requiring minimal collateral. Building on existing partnerships and field collaboration, the current project intends to (1) improve the RCC product to minimize basis risk in product design by incorporating key environmental variables from state-of-the-art remote sensors, along with measurements from weather stations; (2) integrate a gender dimension into RCC analysis by including intra-household and cluster-level randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to reach, benefit, and empower women farmers; (3) develop formal relations with an increasing number of RCC service providers for piloting RCC in Kenya, Zambia, and Ethiopia; and (4) build capacity on risk management through finance and agronomy trainings for farmers in Kenya and Ethiopia, and development of outreach and guidance materials.

description: An integrated framework of global and country Agri-Food Market and Policy Analysis Models (AMPAM) is implemented to assess the potential for and trade-offs associated with scaling interventions and innovations that create jobs, boost incomes, and reduce environmental footprints along food value chains. A key component of AMPAM is the consistent and comparable set of indicators of degrees of policy support to agriculture and food sectors by type of support, food commodities, and countries. This set of policy indicators has been prepared in collaboration with the AgIncentives Consortium (FAO-IFPRI-IDB-OECD-World Bank). Together with the agrifood market database and the AMPAM modeling framework, the policy indicator dataset will be a critical ingredient for the scenario analysis the Initiative will undertake to support decision-makers in assessing the full potential, scalability, market opportunities, priorities for, and trade-offs associated with incentive schemes, and investments and innovations.

description: On-station trials at INERA of shade- and drought-tolerant fast-growing nitrogen-fixing cover crops like Mucuna pruriens and first growing grasses have resulted in increased farm productivity, restoration of degraded lands and soils through improving soil physical, chemical, and biological properties and in banana and coffee systems. Mucuna can also reduce weed burden, improving the quality of life for women and children who provide most of the labor for weeding. Validation trials have also been conducted on farms aligned to large cooperatives/companies. These demonstrations over the year attracted over 800 farmers and partners to learn the soil health enhancement practices and are important demo and learning sites. Lessons from the on-farm testing are informing the innovation finetuning process and on-going scaling process. Studies to capture the agronomic and socio-economic aspects of the innovation, farmers perceptions, innovation uptake and diffusion levels/ process and dis-adoption levels are ongoing to inform the ongoing scaling process.

description: The methodological steps proposed in this guide seek to support the Producers' Association of Leticia and the Canal del Dique in market research. The tool uses a value chain approach to evaluate their current situation or position at the production and business level in the rice chain, their relationships or potential commercial alliances in the primary grains market, and the market or demand for rice in the region of interest for green paddy, dry paddy, white rice, and other by-products. This methodology proposes to approach these issues through qualitative research that combines the collection of secondary information, semi-structured interviews with key actors in the sector, chain mapping exercises, and observation and inquiries at key locations where the product is sold. The methodology aims to strengthen capacities and generate tools that allow access to markets, and has already been applied in the departmentof Bolivar.

description: CGIAR centers pursue a large number of Trait Discovery and Deployment (TD&D) innovations. In 2022 and 2023, a total of 350 and 325 distinct TD&D activities were detailed. The CGIAR TD&D innovation portfolio is focused on biotic stresses (34% in 2022; 41% in 2023); nutritional, production and end-use traits (emphasis of each is between 28% to 30%); abiotic stresses (25%; 22%) and yield per se (10%). Deep-dive sessions at the end of 2024 analyzed use of TD&D results. 74% of all crop teams reported that they seek to introgress between 1-11 traits into elite breeding germplasm. TD&D contributes disease resistance traits (42%), abiotic stress tolerance (21%), production traits (16%), end-use quality (13%) and yield (7%) to active breeding populations. Differences between discovery and deploying genomic resources highlights challenges in finding suitable donor parents and selection methods, more successful for biotic resistance traits, and more challenging for end-use traits.
title: Contributions of CGIAR center crop trait discovery and deployment portfolio to improving resilience, climate change adaptation, nutrition and end-use preferences in crop breeding programs

description: The innovation targeting soybean production in Northern Ghana introduces four key MVPs: site-specific fertilizer recommendations, varietal suitability maps, location-specific maize-soy intercropping systems, and a mechanization platform. These components complement existing digital agronomic, weather, and market advisories, reaching over sixty thousand smallholder farmers. Addressing challenges like limited mechanization, insufficient access to input credit, and low yields, this initiative offers a holistic solution. Features include customized agronomic advice, a digital credit system for inputs, direct linkages to certified input suppliers, and real-time market insights, all delivered through the ESOKO, the demand partner. ESOKO is pivotal in this transformation, providing a user-friendly interface on basic mobile phones, serving as a vital information hub and bridging the gap between farmers and agricultural services. This strategy not only addresses immediate agricultural challenges but also promotes a sustainable, technology-driven ecosystem, enhancing productivity and profitability in Northern Ghana's soybean sector.
title: Supporting sustainable soybean production in Northern Ghana (SSPiNG) through improved agronomic advisory services (GHANA-SOY/ESOKO Use Case)

description: With fertilizer application rates in Africa from the current 20 kg ha−1 to the 50 kg ha−1 target agreed by the Abuja Declaration, food production would have grown by 209% in the last ten years instead of just 24%. description: This innovation converts beans and other nutrient-dense foods into composite flours, addressing major challenges in Africa's food systems. Protein deficiencies affect 26% of African's population, while micronutrient deficiencies like iron and zinc are widespread, with sub-Saharan Africa having the highest rates of anaemia (46%-71%) and vitamin A deficiency (48%) in children under-five. These deficiencies contribute to stunted growth, weakened immunity, and poverty. Traditional bean processing is also labour-intensive and inefficient, limiting the appeal of beans. This innovation improves nutrient absorption by reducing anti-nutritional factors like phytic acid and lectins through techniques such as soaking, malting, roasting and pressure cooking. Instant and regular bean composite flour products also offer extended shelf life, reducing food waste and improving food security. The technology supports small and medium enterprises, fosters economic growth, and strengthens supply chains while improving nutrition across families and communities.

description: Smallholder agricultural mechanization is the call of the day for Africa to improve land and labour productivity, reduce production cost and drudgery, and make agriculture attractive to youth. Successful mechanization in most of African countries relies on selection, validation, piloting, and scaling of appropriate inexpensive machinery solutions adapted to farm size and financial ability of smallholder farmers. Over the past decade, CIMMYT has tested, validated, and piloted small scale machinery and business models suitable for southern African farmers. Based on the experiences and successful piloting, a ‘mechanization starter pack’ has been developed and is recommended for scaling through a business model called the ‘Service Provider Model’. The ‘mechanization starter pack’ includes a two-wheel tractor (2WT), a 2WT operated ripper, a 2WT operated trailer, an engine operated multi-crop thresher, peanut sheller, peanut roaster, peanut butter machine and chopper grinder depending on the farming context of the country. As per the model, a service provider (SP) owns and maintains the machines and operate them on a fee-for-service basis throughout the year benefiting many farmers. The service fee is usually much cheaper for end users (farmers) compared to the cost of traditional practices and creates a win-win situation that makes the business viable for both SP and farmers. The machines chosen for the starter pack allows the SP to generate income throughout the year by providing ploughing, ripping, and threshing/shelling (depending on time of the year), and transportation (year-round) services. Currently there are more than 300 SPs are operating their businesses in Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia benefiting thousands of farmers.

description: This innovation involves incorporation of coarsely-ground Mucuna pruriens grain as a unique, cost-effective ingredient and energy-protein dense substitute in maintenance or fattening rations of ruminant livestock, where standard commercial supplements would usually contain a combination of cereal grains (e.g. maize) and legume oil cakes (e.g Soyabean, cotton seed etc), which are themselves generally expensive.  These expensive ingredients make the commercial concentrates out of reach for most farmers.  In contrast, Mucuna is cheaper and provides both energy and protein in one grain.  Once ground, the Mucuna meal will be constituted together with home-made tropical forage legumes (e.g. Lablab purpureus) hay to make a complete diet which smallholder farmers can brand and trade among themselves. Incorporation of legume hay reduces the amount of poor quality grass hay and cereal crop residues that will be included as basal forage in the complete diet and will simultaneously improve the digestibility of the poor quality residues, leading to improved animal growth.

description: The agrobiodiversity solution hotspot tool is improving understanding of relationships across the food system in India and helping identify priority interventions to restore and enhance ecosystem functions and services for sustainable social and economic benefits. Location-specific threat datasets have been combined with diversity datasets from the Agrobiodiversity Index to create a threat hotspot and agrobiodiversity solution tool for local stakeholders to address water, energy, food and environment (WEFE) challenges. Initially focusing on the Ganges Basin in India, the project has utilized a collaborative approach, co-developing and co-creating with local stakeholders and government partners to develop and refine the tool. This has led to a practical downscaled Agrobiodiversity Index approach that can be used by local stakeholders to address WEFE challenges. Using a locally relevant methodology, the project has prioritized locations to enhance agrobiodiversity, improving agricultural system sustainability and resilience in India. Intensive collaboration took place in India with local and national research and government partners. Due to its methodology, this innovation can be transferred to other geographies.

description: This innovation underpins investment case standardization, implementing a dynamic pipeline developed in 2023 to establish pilot estimates of trait valuation. The approach looks at trait mapping across market segments, leveraging trait experts’ estimation of ultimate benefit of their work to yield benefit and stability. Based on productivity impacts across market segments, additional yield and resulting monetary value are calculated. The framework was applied to 2023 mapped Trait Discovery & Deployment (TD&D) project activities in eleven crops. The analysis highlights the value of investment case standardization and provides valuable input on the need to benchmark estimates in productivity gain, ranging for the same trait from 1% to 15% and 30% to 80% across some programs working on the same TD&D opportunity in the same crop. Leveraging information on investments and understanding the likelihood of success as we advance provides a robust foundation to estimate the relative merit of different TD&D opportunities.

description: The organizational innovation develops tools and approaches for taking stock of current CGIAR breeding pipelines and mapping them to impactful, gender-relevant and gender-intentional, in-demand, feasible target product profiles (TPP’s) - each a unique combination of productivity, adaptation, resilience, quality, processing and consumer traits, that is aligned to a sub-regional market segment, since 2023 using the Breeding Portal. Each TPP contains the traits required and targeted scores. As per November 2024, CGIAR and NARES defined a total of 607 TPPs aligned to Breeding Pipelines and Market Segments. Traits were aligned with 14 distinct value propositions that drive Impact Area tagging of TPPs. Market Intelligence uses the information to develop pipeline investment cases that describe benefits to the five Impact Areas by breeding pipeline. The innovation makes transparent and optimizes the focus of current and new CGIAR breeding pipelines. Through the 2024 review, the quality of TPPs has improved.

description: The innovation seeks to provide an annual update on genetic gains by crop across CGIAR breeding pipelines, using standardized methods.  In 2024, and in alignment with efforts of the ReFOCUS work package, genetic gain estimates were carried out by market segment. Realized genetic gain for yield was reported for 11 crops, 57 pipelines and 107 Market Segments. Realized genetic gains were statistically significant and positive for 62% (66 out of 107) of the studies. Genetic gain estimates of >1% annually were reported for 40% of the market segments. 43% were reported at Early Testing Stage; while 57% were reported using Late Testing Stage data. 58% fully and 32% partially used the recommended check strategy. Genetic gain estimates for 18% of market segments were reported using data from >10 environments per year. Progress can be seen from 2022 and 2023 reports, with more programs and pipelines having reliable genetic gains assessment.
title: A new approach aligns genetic gain assessments of CGIAR breeding pipelines across crops and traits, providing a tool for monitoring the impact of breeding pipeline optimization efforts

description: Crop teams develop new approaches to incorporate farmers' conditions and women and men's views in candidate variety selection, including through citizen science approaches such as Triadic Comparison of Technologies (TRICOT). On-farm trialing is challenged by logistics related to executing representative, hence large-scale and decentralized assessments, and seed multiplication particularly for vegetatively propagated crops. While the individual crop- and pipeline-specific innovations are of technical nature, this result assesses the organizational change across crops. In 2024, 95% of programs carried out on-farm verification in at least one pipeline. The ability to implement minimum quality standards for making advancement decisions almost doubled between 2023 and 2024 when 53% of all programs were able to include 30 or more farms (which would be considered the minimum dataset). 55% of programs collected gender-disaggregated data. Crops increasingly use TRICOT for on-farm trialing both at early-stage testing and during on-farm verification later in the breeding process.
title: Crop-specific approaches for innovative and collaborative on-farm trialing approaches systematically use simpler, yet larger-scale evaluations, and capture gender-disaggregated data, for a more farmer- and market-relevant selection of new crop varieties

description: Considerable efforts are being made by crops to make variety identification schemes more representative of the target population of environments (TPE) and farmers' conditions. Between 2022 and 2024, breeding programs made substantive efforts in aligning breeding schemes with the target product profiles (TPP). 58% of breeding programs reported the extent they are able to measure TPP traits during the different testing stages. The majority can measure around 75% of the essential traits during early testing, allowing higher selection pressures and faster progress. Efforts are on-going to increase this proportion. 89% of the teams have a check strategy in place and 93% made efforts to analyze genotype-by-environment interactions, mostly at Late Testing, to inform their testing strategy. Inclusion of on-farm sites has increased; 32% use it during early testing. These results indicate that breeding programs make significant efforts in making selection environments more representative of the target environments for new varieties.
title: Successful approaches to developing farmer-and market-relevant variety identification schemes increase the emphasis on both precision-phenotyping essential traits and using farmer-representative conditions early in the breeding process

description: Having adequate genetic variance is necessary to make genetic gain. Making genetic gain also means depleting genetic variance. Strategies are needed to augment trait variance in the elite germplasm pool. This variance can come from trait discovery and deployment (TD&D) pipelines, other crop breeding pipelines, or less-related genetic resources. An effective germplasm use strategy aligns breeding pipelines with target product profiles (TPP), understands trait availability viz priorities, and strategically leverages investments across pipelines and organizations. Since 2023, all CGIAR programs use the Breeding Portal to document the Breeding Pipeline - TPP relationships and define the essential traits that need to be improved. During deep-dive sessions in 2024, 74% of programs stated that they introgress between 1 to 11 critical traits into the main breeding pipelines (see Result 1241). There is need to better document and rationalize the TD&D - Breeding Pipeline relationships in the Breeding Portal.
title: The Breeding Portal helps CGIAR crops to optimize pipeline structure and leverage breeding gains within a particular crop, complementing diversity studies and quantitative genetics analytics

description: Innovations under this result include implementing genome-assisted rapid-cycle recurrent selection schemes, more accurate and earlier selection of crossing parents, and rapid advancement approaches, to accelerate the rate of genetic gain in major food crops. End-of-initiative deep-dive sessions with CGIAR breeding teams captured 2022-2024 progress. Currently, cycle time across crops has further reduced to 41 months, going as low as 24 months, with further scope for improvement. Fifty-eight percent of programs use rapid-cycle genomic selection in at least one pipeline, while 32% are establishing genomic selection approaches. This represents significant progress from 2022 and 2023 when only 35% and 45% implemented genomic selection, and cycle times were longer. Use of genomic selection implies and drives that programs also adopt more sophisticated and capable data management systems. Successful models need to be scaled across more breeding pipelines and parameters for estimating breeding value need continuous improvement.
title: CGIAR center experiences with implementing faster and more accurate breeding cycles outline opportunities for more rapidly improving crops most important to farmers in Africa, Asia and Latin America

description: CIP potato breeding harnesses the latest scientific knowledge and tools to develop better varieties. Even though targeted and first tested regionally, the Latin American potato breeding pipelines have significant benefits globally as they pursue: 1. Late blight, heat tolerant potato varieties to enable farmers to cope with climate change. 2. Biofortified potatoes with elevated levels of iron and zinc, and disease and heat resilience traits to reduce malnutrition. Breeding cycle time is 3 years. Selection is for marketable tuber yield and late blight resistance. Biofortified potatoes crosses were made in 2012 between a Peruvian landrace and elite lines with high yield and resistance to prevalent diseases. Twelve clones were selected in collaboration with Peruvian partners and 1600 farmers. Between 2022-2024, partners in China, NIgeria and Peru released 11 varieties, two of them with 37% more iron and 35% more Zinc, contributing to reducing malnutrition.

description: Forage quantity and quality constrain smallholder livestock production in Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Tropical Asia. Improved forages can enhance farm productivity and contribute to the environmental sustainability of crop-livestock systems. Forage breeding seeks to identify niches for forages in a participatory manner, exchanging more productive and resilient farmer-demanded forages between regions. The CIAT breeding program works with four breeding pipelines involving interspecific Urochloa, Urochloa and Megathyrsus types for livestock grazing, and/or cut and carry.  Between 2022-2024, market segments and Target Product Profiles were updated, training populations for genomic selection established, phenotyping accuracy improved, cycle time in Urochloa reduced to 3 years, genotype-by-environment analyses executed, NARS partners trained in using Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS), and public and private sector partners more strongly involved in station and on-farm evaluations. Partners in six countries registered eight new varieties, all of them deriving from pipelines improved for drought and acid soil tolerance.

description: Significant work has been done to understand farmers' and market demands for cassava and incorporate such insights within IITA-CIAT-NARES collaborative breeding programs that pursue greater productivity, disease resistance, and end-use traits. description: Globally, cowpea is cultivated on about 14.5 million hectares. In Africa, cowpea is more of a women's crop. The overall productivity is very low, with average yields ranging from 100 to 400 kg/ha. This is due to several biotic and abiotic constraints. CGIAR-NARES collaborative cowpea breeding seeks to develop higher-yielding, disease- and pest-resilient varieties that meet the requirements in local markets. Breeding pipelines differ by maturity, so to fit different season lengths and cropping systems. They consider that cowpea may be used for both grain and fodder, and both as boiled grain and for making home-made flour. Breeding is a cyclical process with new, further improved varieties forthcoming on a regular basis, building on the feedback of farmers and markets. Large-scale farmer feedback is received using the Triadic-comparison-of-technologies (TRICOT) methodology. Current breeding cycle time is 4 years. Between 2022-2024, partners in four countries registered 35 varieties for use.

description: ICARDA is seeking ways to take advantage of lentil's high nutritional value and low water use that makes it well adapted to cereal-based cropping in dry regions. Focus is on developing improved varieties with heat and drought tolerance, greater productivity and with the ability to mechanize production. Winter hardiness is important for cereal systems. Water-logging tolerance is important in the highlands.  Collaborative breeding activities with public and private sector partners and farmers, pursue the following breeding pipelines: 1. description: Grasspea is a multi-purpose, and hardy legume which can sustain drought, waterlogging and salinity, and can be grown under minimal external inputs. In collaboration with public and private sector partners and farmers, ICARDA breeding efforts are underway to reduce the neurotoxin content in grasspea, while improving its seed yield and biomass, to provide a remunerative crop for safe consumption by humans and animals. The two breeding pipelines pursue 1. Grasspea as a relay no-till crop in rice fields in South Asia, reducing its cost of production. 2. Grasspea as a multipurpose crop for grain, feed, vegetables, and straw, for dry regions in Africa and the Middle East, where its split seeds, flour, and twigs are used for human consumption and fodder, and the plant residues for nutritious animal feed. The current breeding cycle time is 4 years. In 2024, seventy-two advanced lines of were evaluated for yield in diverse environments.

description: Potato is challenged by several biotic stresses including late blight, lowland tropics viruses, bacterial wilt, and nematodes along with abiotic stresses such as heat and drought in South and South-East Asia. CIP initiated a public-private partnership in 2016, in collaboration with partners in Asia and HZPC, a leading private potato seed company, to develop and commercialize early maturing climate-resilient potato varieties for different agro-ecologies and market segments in Asia and Africa. Breeding cycle time is 3.5 years. The tropically adapted advanced clones with late blight and virus resistances were developed using shuttle breeding between highlands and lowland agro-ecologies in Vietnam and the use of molecular markers. The advanced clones are being tested in on-farm trials across major potato-growing areas in lowland and highland agro-ecologies of Vietnam. Between 2022-2024, partners in five countries. registered 53 varieties, 23 in 2024. Nine varieties derived from pipelines improved for heat and drought.

description: Potato is a smallholder cash crop in East and Central African highlands. In many of the drier potato-growing regions, more frequent water and heat stress are leading to declining yields. The East Africa Potato Breeding Network was formalized in May 2023. New candidate varieties are to include resilience traits such as heat tolerance, earliness-to-ripen, virus and late blight resistance, good water-use efficiency. Breeding cycle time is 3-4 years. The resulting varieties are being tested in multilocation trials with public and private partner organizations, and through citizen science approaches with farmers. Even though varieties have been released in the past, recent insights point to yield, taste, marketability, and tuber quality as being most important to farmers. These insights help to adjust target product profiles. Their development is being accelerated through genomic selection, faster cycle times, spatial and GxE analyses that optimize variety testing, and more accurate consumer trait assessments.

description: Sweetpotato breeding seeks to enable 15 million resource‐poor households in Africa and Asia to improve their diets and raise incomes. Since 2022, demand- and gender- responsive target product profiles (TPPs) draw on the input of user studies (Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania), and product design and advancement meetings. description: The CIP sweetpotato breeding program in Peru is serving mostly Asia and Latin America with breeding pipelines for  1. “orange flesh sweet potato (OFSP) for wide adaptation and earliness” suitable for 90 days crop seasons which are in demand in wheat/rice rotation systems, 2. “OFSP with no/low sweetness after cooking” suitable for 120 days crop seasons, and 3. purple-flesh sweetpotatoes for 120 days crop seasons. Genomic tools accelerate the development of more productive, biofortified, consumer-preferred varieties with higher foliage yield. Breeding cycle time is 30 months. description: In collaboration with public and private partners and farmers in South Asia, rice breeding sustainably enhances yields; resilience to pests and diseases; tolerance to drought, salinity, while improving grain and nutritional qualities. description: Rice production in Southeast Asia comprises almost 30% of the World’s rice harvest and produces significant greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. description: Older low-yielding varieties still dominate in large areas of Africa. Farmers are not benefiting quickly enough from genetic gains from recently improved varieties, including those that can withstand climate change related impacts. In collaboration with national research systems, international research partners, and farmers, AfricaRice seeks to provide farmers with superior, market-demanded rice varieties, adapted to local growing conditions. The rich reservoir of genetic resources present in the indigenous Africa rice germplasm pool is combined with modern breeding approaches to increase the rate of genetic gains. Current breeding cycle time is 36 months. Eight breeding pipelines target sixteen market segments, encompassing about 12.6 M ha of rice area. In 2023, target product profiles were validated with stakeholders in 10 countries. 20 African countries routinely assess candidate varieties that identify those most likely to meet farmers' needs. Between 2022-2024, partners in 15 countries registered 60 varieties, 43 selected for climate resilience traits.

description: Common beans are an important staple food for more than 200 million Africans, providing an affordable source of proteins, complex carbohydrates and valuable micronutrients. They improve soil fertility and are a significant source of income. In collaboration with the Pan Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA) and farmers, CIAT and national bean breeding efforts seek to develop improved and marketable bush and climbing bean varieties. The program builds on past progress on progress in resistance to bean diseases and tolerance to drought. Current emphasis is on gender intentional traits, biofortification for zinc and iron, and reducing cooking time. Breeding is a cyclical process that adjusts to feedback from farmers, seed companies and end-users. Breeding cycle time is 24 months. Between 2022 and 2024, partners in 20 countries tested and registered 79 bean varieties (25 in 2024) that were collaboratively developed between local breeding programs and CIAT.

description: The CIMMYT Global Wheat Program is one of the most important public sources of high yielding, nutritious, disease- and climate-resilient wheat varieties for Africa, Asia, and Latin America; its lines are found in varieties sown on more than 60 million hectares worldwide. The program works with ICARDA and more than 200 local research and breeding institutions, sharing climate-resilient, Zinc-biofortified, high- yielding, disease and pest tolerant wheat lines and data. description: In collaboration with national yam breeding programs in Nigeria, Cote d’Ivoire, Ghana and Benin, IITA yam breeding seeks to develop and deploy end-user preferred White Yam and Water Yam varieties with higher yield, greater resistance to pests and diseases and improved quality, targeted at West Africa. description:
We describe an approach for incentivizing nature-positive farming practices, comprising of: (1) Best-Worst Scaling workshops to identify farmers' preferred practices, (2) Collecting competitive group tender bids from interested farmer groups for implementing the practices. Groups quantify their targets for implementation, and determine the in-kind compensation they require in return of ecosystem service provision, (3) Technical guidance in implementing the practices, (4) Distribution of the agreed rewards upon successful completion._x000D_
We applied the approach with indigenous farmers from in four communes in Northern Vietnam. Most preferred practices were improving agrobiodiversity by integrating native trees in farming systems and restoring erosion-prone lands through tree planting. In total 11 bids involving 81 farmers from 9 villages were selected for implementation, based on e.g. cost per area restored, species choices, and equity considerations (e.g. gender balance). In total 52 hectares were restored, 18,270 trees planted, 3 smallholder nurseries established, and rewards worth US$11,578 paid out.
title: Payments for Ecosystem Services tender approach for Incentivizing nature-positive farming practices in Northern Vietnam

description: The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) builds on the work of the Sustainable Intensification Innovation Lab (SIIL) Project in Bangladesh through the International Rice Research Institute. Their joint efforts aim to implement a transformative project in the polder zone, targeting the untapped agricultural production potential of the region. Currently, the rice-rice production system was introduced in the southcentral (SC) and southwest (SW) coastal zones to increase land productivity. Since river water remain non-saline in most rivers of SC region, the farmer pumped water from the polder canals that entered inside the polders during high tides. While the river water becomes saline in the dry season in SW region and the farmers utilized groundwater (where salinity permits) for rice irrigation.  The farmers cultivated climate-resilient, nutritious and salt-tolerant HYV rice in both wet and dry seasons and harvested 10-12 t/ha/yr that significantly contributed to their food security.

description: Researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets and Resilient Cities collaborated on the design of an innovation in 2024, which will be implemented and tested starting in 2025 in collaboration with the Food Systems for Nutrition Innovation Lab. The intervention will work at the interface between market provision and consumer demand to support markets to deliver safe food and promote healthier diets. The team will design and measure the effectiveness and costs of a synergistic vendor- and consumer-oriented strategy to improve food safety and the livelihoods of food vendors and to improve the diets of adult women of child-bearing age and children under 5 years from low- and middle-income families in Dhaka. Two synergistic approaches will be used: a market-oriented strategy that strengthens wet markets and the associated informal food vendors to deliver safe and nutritious diets and a consumer-oriented intervention that empowers and encourages consumers to demand safer and higher-quality foods.

description: ICRISAT's commitment to chickpea breeding has led to significant breakthroughs, focusing on developing varieties that are high-yielding and resilient to environmental challenges, especially drought. Currently, yield, end use quality, drought and heat tolerance, and resistant to Fusarium wilt and Ascochyta blight resistance are being improved in four pipelines targeting different Desi and Kabuli market segments in each subregion. Current cycle time is between 36 and 48 months with the intent to accelerate through speed-breeding. Genomic selection is being established for 100-seed weight, days to maturity, plant height, and pods per plant. High-throughput phenotyping approaches and breeding schemes are being improved to access greater genetic variance, increase selection intensity and accelerate genetic gains. Multi-environment trials cover up to 20 environments. Genetic resources are being explored for resistance to Ascochyta blight diseases and Fusarium wilt, and higher protein contents. Between 2022 and 2023, partners in India registered three chickpea varieties.

description: To meet the ambition of increasing the rate of genetic gain for key traits in preferred and climate-resilient crop varieties, breeders must make accurate, data-driven decisions quickly. Achieving this requires analyzing large volumes of data from different sources to account for variances arising from breeding populations, environmental conditions, and farm management practices - the genotype-by-environment-by-management (GxExM) complex. This comprehensive approach ensures the selection of fit-for-purpose candidate varieties. To support this effort, Breeding Resources, in collaboration with Accelerated Breeding, developed a breeding analytics and decision-support tool that enables CGIAR-National Agricultural Research and Extension Services (NARES) breeders to access data from different sources, analyze it rapidly, and make informed decisions about which genotypes to recycle as new parents for the next cycle and which to advance as candidate varieties. The tool incorporates modules essential for breeders to conduct comprehensive genetic evaluations of test genotypes, driving efficiency and precision in the breeding process.
title: Biometrical Genetics Workflow (Bioflow): CGIAR-NARES breeding analytics and decision support tool designed to enable faster decisions, accelerate breeding cycles, and increase genetic gains

A ShareFair is an interactive and collaborative event designed to facilitate the exchange of knowledge, innovations, and best practices among diverse stakeholders. Bringing together practitioners, policymakers, researchers, and community representatives, a ShareFair creates a dynamic space for learning, networking, and co-creation. The format includes thematic sessions, hands-on demonstrations, open discussions, and storytelling, offering participants an opportunity to explore tools and approaches in areas such as sustainable development, agriculture, and knowledge management._x000D_
_x000D_
Focused on inclusivity, ShareFairs emphasize local knowledge, cross-sectoral collaboration, and practical solutions. They often integrate both traditional methods and digital tools, creating a balance between face-to-face engagement and technology-mediated interaction. Participants leave equipped with actionable insights, new partnerships, and strategies for addressing pressing challenges in their respective fields. By fostering a culture of shared learning, ShareFairs promote the collective advancement of ideas and innovations for sustainable impact.

description:
The BRIGHT survey contains several innovations that aim to uncover new insights into important survey methodology issues and shed light on intra-household resource allocation and gender and age differences in individuals’ perceptions on various household welfare dimensions. The two main innovations are:_x000D_
1) Randomization of the subjective household wellbeing module: Both female and male respondents randomly receive this module and at three different points during the interview. By randomizing the households' respondents, gender differences in the subjective assessment of household wellbeing can be examined. By randomizing the placement of the module, the sensitivity of reported wellbeing levels to topics surveyed prior to the assessment can be analyzed._x000D_
2) Duplication of several modules in the male and female respondent parts, as well as in the parts to multiple respondents of the same gender. These include the employment module where the man responds for himself, and the female responds for herself and all of the other household members; the women’s empowerment module, where both respondents answer questions on empowerment; the debt and savings module, where both respondents answer questions on their own savings; and the food-away-from-home consumption module, where female and male respondents answer questions for their families and their spouses. This innovation allows researchers to analyze intra-household gender and age differences in perceptions on the surveyed topics._x000D_
Other innovations include two versions of a water security scale, as well as an energy security scale. This allows researchers to examine which version performs better in capturing access to and quality of water and energy, respectively.  The new modules incorporated in the survey allow for a more granular analysis of various poverty dimensions

description: My Farm Trees is a digital tool for the documentation, verification and quality control of tree seed supply networks for agroforestry and land restoration, and for connecting and rewarding network actors for ecosystem services. It uses blockchain to create a transparent link of information from seed collection to tree growth – to improve livelihoods, food security and climate change mitigation. A module of the tool was developed for Laos, including 188 local tree species with their scientific, Lao and local names. The tool allows farmers to document and report their efforts on integrating trees in silvopastoral and other mixed farming systems, to access payments for ecosystem services

description: The scaling business model is proposed based on approaches as suggested by Lundy et al. (2012) that includes three major steps. First, mapping the existing business model using the nine caveats and identifying major challenges and opportunities. The existing business model was mapped using data from baseline and marketing assessment surveys focusing on inputs supply, production, marketing, institutional support, vertical and horizontal coordination along the value chain. Second, identifying business cases using lessons learned from previous tropical poultry genetics solution activities in Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Third, developing the new business model considering the business cases identified above. The proposed scaling business model has six  major components: establishing partnership, organizing and building capacity, access to inputs and services (i.e . feed, heath, finance, breed, training and extension services), production and support, value addition and marketing (through aggregators, wholesalers, retailers and processors), monitoring and optimization.

description:
Cassava previously lacked genomic resources representing both copies of its heterozygous diploid genome and species-wide diversity. This limited variant discovery and accurate prediction of missing sequence (imputation) in breeders sequence data. Previous sequence data also had high error rates hampering detection of variants linked or causal to agronomic and end-use traits. _x000D_
_x000D_
The cassava practical haplotype graph was created using newly generated highly accurate sequence data for 52 taxa, yielding 104 assemblies representing both genome copies and phased along chromosomes. Taxa represent elite breeding parents, disease resistant materials, and diverse landraces from Latin America and Africa._x000D_
_x000D_
The practical haplotype graph provides the assemblies, alignments, and variant calls in a compact, shareable format and provides tools to impute and call variants from inexpensive sequence data. The resource is already being applied to new DNA language models to identify variants for improved yield and disease resistance and to further improve imputation accuracy.
title: Cassava practical haplotype graph, a pan-genomic resource capturing complete DNA sequence variation across cultivated cassava, enabling breeders to utilize genetic variation causal to important crop traits for agricultural improvement.

description: This study addresses key challenges in integrating genomic-enabled prediction into sweetpotato breeding, particularly genotype-by-environment interactions and constructing effective training sets. Two hypotheses were tested : (i) using deregressed ABLUPs (dABLUPs-best linear unbiased prediction from the animal model) in two-stage modeling improves predictive accuracy in observational trials, and (ii) optimizing training sets can reduce experimental effort while maintaining accuracy. Evaluating 1185 genotypes across six trials in Uganda and comparing four modeling approaches, dABLUPs consistently provided the best predictions, improving predictive ability by up to 37% over other methods. Optimized training sets further enhanced performance, demonstrating the potential for more efficient genomic prediction in sweetpotato breeding.
title: Enhanced predictive accuracy and efficiency in genomic-assisted sweetpotato breeding using deregressed best linear unbiased prediction (BLUPs) from the animal model and optimized training populations

description: Traditionally, homegardens have been essential for ensuring access to healthy food and conserving local biodiversity. However, their application in intensive systems like Amazonian cacao cultivation, which requires specialized labor, has been limited. The high dependence on cacao exposes families to economic risks. To diversify production and improve food security, we propose co-creating family gardens based on agroecological practices, selecting complementary crops to ensure a stable supply of healthy food.

description: Technoserve is managing Horticulture for Growth, a program designed to improve food systems in specific sites across Ethiopia. As a complement to this program, researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets and NEED Nutritional Products and Services, have been developing a bundled intervention for vendors and consumers to test how a combination of coupons, visual branding, food safety and nutrition education, and other video-based behavior change communication strategies can increase consumer demand for fruits and vegetables and stimulate vendors to make improvements in their sales of fruits and vegetables. NEED will implement the intervention and researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets will conduct the evaluation in a combination of urban, peri-urban, and urban sites in Ethiopia. The discussions and written plans reached a promising stage by the end of 2024. Work is expected to begin in 2025.

description: In Senegal, approximately 10,000,000 baguettes of bread are consumed every day. Almost all of this bread is produced from wheat, a cereal imported and subsidized by the State of Senegal. This generates expenses of several billion CFA francs per year, representing a considerable loss of income for local sectors and small producers. However, agri-food research has shown that it is possible to produce compound bread, incorporating a high percentage of local cereals, such as millet. Although naturally gluten-free, millet can be used effectively in bread making. The Senegalese Institute of Agricultural Research (ISRA) has developed short-cycle millet varieties, adapted to climate change and producing large grains, ideal for flour production, thus meeting the needs of millers and bakers. It is in this context that we are developing compound bread, with an incorporation rate of 30% millet, making it possible to reduce wheat imports by the same proportion. In the past, millet was mainly sold raw in markets, without adding value. Thanks to this innovation, millet is now processed locally, contributing to wealth creation, reducing imports and generating jobs in local communities.
title: Agroecology business model for the reduction of imports: production of composite bread incorporating 30% millet as a substitute for wheat

description:
The introduction of a Geographical Indication (GI) for local olive oil in Ellès-Sers is an innovative labeling approach to valorizing the diversity of local cultivars and highlighting the region's unique olive oil characteristics. This initiative empowers small farmers, who primarily use traditional agronomic practices, by protecting their local expertise rooted in sustainable practices._x000D_
Focusing on agro-ecological specialization offers significant advantages for the community, safeguarding the historical significance of this olive-growing site as part of Tunisia's heritage. With its multi-centenarian plantations of ancestral cultivars, Ellès-Sers can maintain its distinct identity while developing a competitive business model._x000D_
By forming farmer organizations, producers can collaborate to enhance the value of their olive oils and promote regional knowledge, positioning olive oil as a catalyst for rural development and economic growth while preserving cultural heritage.

description: Leguminous forage crops, including sulla, faba beans, and vetch, establish symbiotic relationships with specific Rhizobia bacteria in their root nodules, enabling biological nitrogen fixation. This innovation involves inoculating forage legume seeds with carefully selected rhizobia strains tailored to crop species and local environmental conditions. The specific Rhizobia bacteria enhanced nitrogen fixation, leading to improved biomass yield, superior forage quality ( higher protein content), and increased crop resilience. Post-harvest, residual fixed nitrogen enriches the soil, benefiting subsequent crops like cereals by reducing the need for synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. This reduces production costs for farmers, improves soil fertility, and minimizes the ecological impact of agriculture. By integrating rhizobial inoculation into forage crop systems,  this innovation promotes sustainable agricultural practices while supporting soil health, crop productivity, and long-term agroecological balance.
title: Rhizobial inoculation of forage legume seeds in Tunisia to enhance symbiotic nitrogen fixation, increase biomass production and promote sustainable agroecological practices in forage systems

description:
In Tunisia, some of the main constraints in crop-livestock production systems are the monoculture of cereals, which leads to poor soil health, and lack of nutrient-rich forages to keep small ruminants in good health. _x000D_
Some forage mixtures (Vetch-Oat, Vetch-Triticale, Vetch-Oat - Triticale), are being pre-defined and recommended by the research team composed of INRAT (Institut National de Recherche Agronomique de Tunis), Office of livestock and pasture (OEP) and ICARDA. Different combinations for forage seed mixture are tested in different climatic  and soil contexts, and recommendations are provided to a private seed company COTUGRAIN, to tailor its seed mixtures products for commercialization.

description: The biochar technology, whereby organic materiel like olive branches are carbonized through a slow burning process is a low cost technology for small scale farmers. Its major effects are the improvement of soil structure through crumb structure formation, increasing water holding capacity and reduction of need and improved efficiency of mineral fertilizers. It is therefore a well adapted technology in semi-arid areas were rainfall is scarce and improved efficiency of water use is important to increase yields of field crops and trees. The technology is well adapted for small-scale farmers in olive - cereal based production systems where you have abandoned olive tree branches after pruning for processing into biochar. Biochar can be used to increase wheat production as the major and most profitable cereal crop grown in North-West Tunisia

description: The CGIAR  2030 Research and Innovation Strategy advances “a new strategy to address new challenges” for “transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis”. Operationalizing this strategy necessitates tracking performance across ﬁve deﬁned Impact Areas: Nutrition, Health and Food Security; Poverty Reduction, Livelihoods, and Jobs; Gender Equality, Youth, and Social Inclusion; Climate Adaptation and Mitigation; and Environmental Health and Biodiversity. CGIAR does not yet have a set of performance measures ﬁt for this purpose. This collaborative innovation between CGIAR and scientists at Cornell University aims to conceptualize, develop and prototype a comprehensive agrifood systems performance measurement system to meet this need.

description: Sustainable Healthy Diets researchers from Wageningen University and Research designed an online interactive tool ("dashboard") for policymakers in Bangladesh. The online tool allows users to dive deeper into the results from a foresight study analyzing the trade-offs between environmental, health and socio-economic indicators of different food scenarios in Bangladesh up to 2040 and 2050. The researchers used MAGNET, a global economic model. They compared a business-as-usual (BAU) diet to a planetary health diet scenario, which aligns with the diet proposed by the EAT-Lancet Commission, ("the EAT-Lancet diet"), and the Bangladesh food-based dietary guidelines (FBDG). The online tool is part of this Initiative's work to promote the use of decision-support tools that stakeholders can use to navigate food system trade-offs in a fairer, more inclusive and more equitable way.
title: Online, interactive tool to provide policymakers with easy access to the results of trade-off modelling from Bangladesh

description: The main dairy product consumed by the population of Bobo-Dioulasso is yogurt. The majority of dairies make yogurts based on imported milk powder and flavor the yogurts with artificial flavors. The Bobo-Dioulasso dairies that are members of ALL and that process locally produced fresh milk have started to diversify their yogurt production by flavoring them with natural extracts of non-timber forest products and local agricultural products (pineapple, sweet banana (poyo), coconut, date, ginger, horchata (chufa), kinkéliba, mango, mint, moringa, nere, monkey bread (théodo), orange-fleshed sweet potato, tamarind, zeguene (balanites)). And it works. There is an outlet for these yogurts that we can qualify as ''agroecological yogurts'' because they are made from real milk and flavored with local natural flavors.
title: Yogurts made from local milk and flavored with natural extracts from local non-timber forest products and agricultural products to foster new business models for improved livelihoods in Burkina Faso

description: In Bobo-Dioulasso (Burkina Faso), dairy farmers have a growing need for quality fodder. Faced with an inadequate local market for forage seeds, dairy industry stakeholders operating under a Dairy Innovation Platform (DIP) have been experimenting with a forage seed production and sharing system based on cooperation between dairy farmers. Mother dairy farmers set up a Fodder Demo-Plot on their farm consisting of 4 forage crops (maize, sorghum, cowpea and mucuna). For each crop, 2/3 of the FDP's area was dedicated to forage production and the remaining 1/3 to seed production. Seeds produced are divided into three equal parts between the 'mother farmer' and two 'babies farmers' with a view to introducing three FDPs in year n+1.
title: Cooperative forage seed production and sharing system among dairy farmers of Bobo-Dioulasso (Burkina Faso)

For each crop, 2/3 of the FDP's area was dedicated to forage production and the remaining 1/3 to seed production. Seeds produced are divided into three equal parts between the 'mother farmer' and two 'babies farmers' with a view to introducing three FDPs in year n+1. description: Global interest in the need to transform food systems to protect human and planetary health provides a major opportunity for improving nutrition in tandem with achieving other societal goals. Ensuring that food systems transformation truly leads to sustainable healthy diets for all requires a much stronger evidence base than what is currently available. Policymakers, funders, implementing partners, and researchers are looking for credible evidence about what works to guide food systems transformation in better directions. The guidance draws on six program evaluations from Africa and South Asia, experts, including one from Sustainable Healthy Diets, and provides six recommendations for designing better evaluations of food system interventions. Better evaluation methodologies for such complex studies can generate the evidence that is urgently needed to support the ambitious goals of food systems transformation.

description: In Bangladesh, it is primarily cultivated by smallholder farmers, with a growing focus on biofortified and early bulking varieties to combat malnutrition and improve yields. This study evaluated the yield performance and adaptability of early bulking sweet potato genotypes across different environments in Bangladesh using advanced yield trials. The AMMI (Additive Main Effects and Multiplicative Interaction) and joint regression analyses were conducted to assess genotype-by-environment interactions. The results indicated that genotype and environment significantly influenced sweet potato performance, with check variety SP12 exhibiting the highest yield. However, the assessment of viral disease incidence revealed that all the studied genotypes were susceptible to significant viral infections, which could undermine their overall viability in production systems. Consequently, while genotypes P4-22 and P2-551 demonstrated adaptability across environments, their severe susceptibility to virus diseases highlights the need to replicate the trials with clean material in the next season for a definitive conclusion.

description: CGIAR and Wageningen University developed a series of approaches, tools and products aimed at strengthening scaling performance in the Research for Development (R4D) sector, including Scaling Readiness and GenderUp for Scaling. For these and other tools to be used widely in the CGIAR system and broader R4D sector, developing individual and team capacity at scale is essential. Several capacity development products have been developed and are being delivered. Examples include the online course on innovation and scaling, Scaling Readiness Training of Facilitators workshops, GenderUp facilitator training, and a course for innovating and scaling for social transformation in international food systems. However, CGIAR developers of these capacity development products have limited bandwidth to deliver these trainings at the required scale R4D organizations. We want to explore modalities where other organizations that could deliver these trainings cheaper, at the required scale, and in a sustainable way.

description: Environmental flow (e-flow) assessments are crucial for understanding river health, flow dynamics, and ecosystem interactions. They guide water management decisions to balance ecological sustainability with human water needs, benefiting researchers and policymakers. To improve e-flow assessments, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and GroundTruth, under the CGIAR Initiative on Digital Innovation, have developed an advanced, less labor-intensive approach using drones and tethered survey vessels equipped with LiDAR and SoNAR sensors. This system captures high-resolution, near real-time hydrological and habitat data over vast areas, surpassing traditional manual surveys. By integrating these data into a digital twin of the Limpopo River Basin, researchers can model river flow, sediment transport, and aquatic habitats with unprecedented accuracy. This innovation enhances decision-making for water resource management, enabling proactive responses to environmental changes and ensuring the sustainable stewardship of vital river ecosystems.

description: The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) has developed the highly versatile Cas-CLOVER system as an alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 for gene editing in banana. The Cas-CLOVER system operates through a dimeric mechanism, utilizing two guide Ribonucleic acid (RNA) and the Clo051 endonuclease, and has proven effective in inducing mutations across a variety of plant species, including banana. In light of intellectual property (IP) concerns and licensing challenges associated with CRISPR/Cas9, the Cas-CLOVER system offers a valuable alternative for gene editing in crops like banana.  We are currently developing excision tools, such as the piggyBac system, to enable the creation of transgene-free bananas using Cas-CLOVER, ensuring that no foreign genetic material remains in the edited plants.

description: Postharvest losses are a global challenge, and fragile fruits, such as tomatoes, often suffer significant losses. In response, FRESH researchers are exploring a novel approach to packaging and transporting tomatoes. In the Philippines, a collaboration between he University of Philippines Mindanao and FRESH core partner Applied Horticultural Research aimed to mitigate losses by experimenting with simple yet effective interventions. The focus was on preventing physical damage from tight stacking, a practice compromising nutritional value and increasing susceptibility to diseases. The solution involves double-lining crates with newspaper before packing and implementing a quality grading scale. Trials in diverse storage conditions consistently demonstrated that tomatoes handled with these improved methods outperformed traditionally managed ones, exhibiting higher quality, reduced disease incidence, and enhanced visual appeal. Preliminary trials in Tanzania are underway, anticipating that the potential benefits, including improved quality, reduced wastage, and extended shelf life, will outweigh initial transportation cost increases.
title: Low-cost solutions to improve tomato transport and storage
