description: This is an institutional innovation development in which the regional network on gender and plant heath was established in Southeast Asia as a model case with a potential to expand to other regions. This network enables the plant health initiative to mainstream gender as a key research agenda towards gender equitable and inclusive technology adoption and scaling. 50 members from 34 institutions in 8 countries joined the network, 80% of them are pathologists, entomologists or agronomists. The first face-to-face workshop was held in Bali in December to identify priority research areas, and gain gender-responsive research knowledge and skills. Six cross-country, interdisciplinary research proposals were developed with a primary focus on gender-related research questions: Maize fall armyworm, Banana fusarium, tomato diseases, mango fruit fly, rice pests and diseases, poultry New Castle disease. The plant health initiative will offer regular support and online meetings to strengthen their research capacity and implementation.

description: Accurate reporting of livestock greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is important in developing effective mitigation strategies. This innovation is a set of  activity data collection protocols to collect animal activity data on-farm and calculate GHG emission factors for enteric methane from cattle and small ruminants which can be applied in smallholder and pastoral livestock systems in Africa. Animal activity data include parameters such as animal numbers, herd composition, animal live weight, feed quality and quantity, manure management, and others. The protocols also describe the equations needed to calculate GHG emission factors. These emission factors can be used to develop national livestock GHG inventories on a Tier 2 level (i.e., with country-specific data) and to test the GHG mitigation potential of management interventions.
title: Protocols to develop country-specific livestock greenhouse gas emission factors in smallholder and pastoral systems in Africa south of the Sahara

description: NARES breeding programs and seed multiplication and delivery are two different entities that show little integration. The so called “hand-over point” is of crucial importance and a poorly developed bottleneck in the chain. The NARES departments that are responsible for seed multiplication and delivery are poorly equipped with strategic tools to plan seed delivery and feed information back to breeders. This action-oriented systematic approach aims to be a tool (a guideline) for the NARES to fill this gap. It consists of different components that need to be brought in line with each other - through iteration (if the budget needed for the first draft plan is too high, the number of selected regions/target groups to whom to distribute seed of the (new, cleaned) variety needs to be adjusted, to finally match available budget, etc. etc.).
title: Systematic approach for national seed system stakeholders to understand seed demand and inform delivery pathways: a protocol to follow for data collection and systematization..

description: Seed production can benefit women as an enterprise and can, at the same time, strengthen their key roles in seed systems (Puskur et al., 2021). description: A draft report has been completed describing the methodology to spatially link vegetatively-propagated crop seed production and the demand for that seed. Previous geo-referenced datasets for cassava seed entrepreneurs in Tanzania have been expanded to include sweetpotato seed producers in Uganda, Tanzania and Kenya. Production maps have been generated for banana, cassava, sweetpotato and yam as well as an Africa-wide map illustrating average travel time to urban markets. These datasets have been used to construct a preliminary map illustrating seed demand for cassava in East Africa. This users of this innovation will be national seed system actors, including national research systems, regulatory agencies as well as private seed producers and buyers. The tool will be included within the Seed Tracker app that will be freely accessible through the www.seedtracker.org website.

description: Using a multicriteria analysis assessment approach, data from experiments conducted by CSISA with BRRI, in alignment with TAFSSA, showed that compared to puddled transplanted rice, both direct-seeded rice (DSR) methods (direct machine drilling and broadcasting) reduced production costs, labor use, specific energy, and total and yield-scaled global warming potential. In addition, DSR had higher energy use efficiency and similar productivity. Performance for direct seeded rice was best when established with a two-wheeled tractor seed drill, and where established on highland or medium highland where flood water in the early spring aus rice season could not damage emerging seedlings after stand establishment. These recommendations have been passed on to the Department of Agricultural Extension as a suite of recommendations used by extension agents to advise farmers on how to grow DSR rice.

description: The lack of systematic tools for measuring climate change adaptation limits progress assessment toward the goals of the Paris Agreement. To address this gap, we introduce the Biomass Climate Adaptation Index (Biomass CAI) as a novel approach to measure agricultural climate adaptation progress at various scales. This method models time series of Vegetation Index (VI) for seasonal cropland, including both smallholders and larger industrial crops, and accounting for external factors like weather and past VI trends. Predictions of greenness, incorporating current weather impact and calibrated over a two-decade baseline, are compared with satellite-measured values using a synthetic counterfactual approach. Deviations suggest improvements or deterioration in agricultural status, informing adaptation progress and intervention needs. Although implemented in Sub-Saharan Africa, in an area ranging from Senegal to Ethiopia, it lacks thorough validation beyond small-scale studies. The Biomass CAI focuses on decision-support to maximize impact of adaptation investments and interventions in agricultural lands.
title: Biomass Climate Adaptation Index (CAI): A satellite-based near real-time climate adaptation monitoring system

description: The International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) methodological guidance recommends countries report the uncertainty of their greenhouse gas inventories. However, uncertainty is practically never reported due to a lack of knowledge of the appropriate methods available. In collaboration with demand and scaling partner, the New Zeland Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Center (NZAGRIC), in support of the Greenhouse Gas Research Alliance Livestock Research Group, the Livestock and Climate Initiative is designing, piloting, and scaling a tool to automate uncertainty calculations based on user-supplied input data. This greenhouse gas uncertainty calculator is programmed in R and will be built into an interactive app (i.e., Shiny).  The tool is intended to be used by national government employees who prepare and have responsibility for submitting greenhouse gas inventories.
title: Uncertainty calculator for national government livestock greenhouse gas emission inventories

title: Climate Security Proofing Guidelines for Livestock Production Systems: a guide for peace proof climate action

Intended users are development and humanitarian actors implementing or planning to implement projects in areas of conflict or are prone to conflict.  This framework will offer different actors adequate guidance to understand of the contexts and identify appropriate strategies for programming that integrate climate action and peacebuilding approaches. Moreover, applying this framework can inform the design and implementation of integrated programming recommendations for specific contexts, improving interventions to mitigate and prevent conflicts and reduce people’s inequalities and vulnerabilities. Climate Security Proofing Guidelines for Livestock Production Systems: a guide for peace proof climate action

description: Various information and communication tools are used in two-way advisory services to interact with farmers. However, the utility and impact of such interactions are not well understood, primarily due to the lack of quality data at scale. To advance knowledge, we are developing a spatiotemporal prediction model of agricultural information demand in India by analyzing communications between farmers and the Kisan Call Centers. As the early stage of innovation, we processed more than 30 million records of communications that took place between 2004 and 2022 and validated macro trends in the data. We are further analyzing this database to identify spatiotemporal patterns of information needs, linking with explanatory variables such as climate and market trends that appear to trigger certain types of risks. Once fully analyzed, we anticipate the model can predict future systemic shocks in advance and help decision-makers prepare for measures to manage the risks in advance.
title: An Artificial Intelligence-based farmers' agricultural information demand prediction model for digital extension services in India

description: This innovation seeks to increase production of energy and protein-dense livestock feed products / ingredients from maize-based farming systems in sub-humid agro-climatic regions of southern Africa. This will be achieved through sustainable intensification practices that involve adoption of improved forage legumes varieties by smallholder farmers.  Specifically the innovation will  provide site-specific advice to farmers and agricultural extension staff on climate smart, annual (or weakly biennial) forage legumes varieties of Lablab purpureus (Lablab), Mucuna pruriens (Velvet beans) and Vigna anguiculata (Cowpeas) that can be intercropped or grown in rotation with maize to produce forage and  grain products or by-products, which will be used as ingredients in manufacture of commercial and home-mixed feed rations for beef, dairy and small-stock production. Forage-based feeds are more accessible and cost-effective to smallholder farmers.  As such, they would be suitable replacements for the largely expensive commercial supplements supplied by private sector companies, which have generally been poorly adopted by the smallholder farmers.
title: Mixed cultivation or ley-cropping of forage legumes with maize to achieve high yields of grain, green fodder and residue to feed livestock

description: Feeding green manure/cover crops (GMCCs) to livestock is an innovative way of improving livestock productivity while attaining other benefits. GMCCs are plants that are grown in cropping systems not primarily for their grain but to provide groundcover, feed, and fertilize the soil. In most cases green manures are legumes that fix nitrogen from the air and, once killed by rolling, spraying, or uprooting, provide large amounts of biomass. This biomass can be used to feed livestock amongst other uses. GMCCs may be grown either as rotational crops or as intercrops with the main crop. When they are introduced as intercrops, they are commonly killed before introducing the next main crop. GMCCs have different growth habits and hence give different benefits depending on their characteristics. They also may serve different purposes in the farming systems depending on their local context.

description: Groundnut breeding targeted at eastern and southern Africa continues the work that ICRISAT has been doing under CIMMYT leadership, and in collaboration with Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia.  The network has three pipelines and target product profiles (TPPs): 1. Short duration tan groundnuts for food and food processing; 2/3. Medium duration resilient red or tan groundnuts for food processing, confectionery flour, and snacks. During 2023, the network jointly reviewed trait priorities to be pursued through breeding. Country product design teams were formed; 30% of members are women. Breeding program assessment were conducted in Tanzania, Sudan, Malawi and Mozambique, to assess how to best include NARES  strengths and capabilities in collaborative germplasm development. The key elements of effective breeding pipelines are being  implemented including: high-throughput phenotyping, rapid cycling of early generation germplasm, simulations to optimize NARES and CG breeding schemas, and joint evaluations and variety identification.
title: Groundnut breeding network in eastern and southern Africa accelerates genetic gains for improved varieties that serve three newly defined market segments and deploy modern optimization, cycling and phenotyping practices.

description: A new conceptual framework to assess opportunities for research engagement in the policy process, building upon existing understandings of power dynamics and the political economy of policy reform. The new framework is based on four principles needed to design research that enables constructive engagement in policy processes: (a) nurture multi-stakeholder coalitions for change at different points in the policy cycle, (b) engage a range of forms and spaces of power, (c) embed research communications to support and respond to dialogue, and (d) employ evaluation in a cycle of action, learning, and adaptation. The framework and principles can be used to identify entry points for research engagement and to reflect critically upon the choices that researchers make as actors within complex processes of change.

description: FishBase, launched in 1990, is the web's largest and most widely used online database of adult finfish. The annual cost of keeping FishBase online and the information updated is approximately $350,000 – entirely derived through arduous fundraising and insufficient to modernize the website. Blockchain, cryptography, and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) could be the means to sustainably fund FishBase as they offer the possibility to capture economic value from the global community that uses and benefits from the data produced by FishBase.
title: Digital solution for the economic sustainability of aquatic ecosystems/databases using blockchain, cryptography and non-refungible tokens

description: The report highlights innovative ways through radical collaborations to achieve climate justice for women, girls and marginalized communities. One route to solutions is through partnerships, between governments and development partners and community-based women’s groups and networks, that give equal voice to women from low-income, climate-affected communities to define climate and water problems and solutions. Such collaborations would, despite their obvious merit, be ‘radical’ because women in climate-affected communities today often are regarded as mere ‘beneficiaries’. However, our experience shows that given the space and resources to do so, women can lead innovation on climate solutions.

description: Blast, caused by the fungus Pyricularia oryzae is one of the most economically important diseases of rice. Leaf blast and neck blast are considered the most important forms of the disease. Surveys conducted in the Philippines from 2014 to the present showed the increased prevalence and incidence of blast compared to the 1990s. Simulation modeling will improve the timing and effectiveness of management strategies and tactics, identify the most important risk factors and reduce yield losses. The weather-driven disease models were developed and then coupled based on empirical evidence that plant tissues with leaf blast serve as a source of inoculum for neck blast. Models of both diseases have been published but have not been previously coupled. A user-friendly interface was created for simulating disease progress curves and mapping simulated epidemics. The models are being improved and validated based on the results of ongoing field experiments and published literature.
title: Simulation modelling of leaf blast and neck blast epidemics

description: A short, animated video was produced by CGIAR researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets, Wageningen University and Research (WUR), and the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) of Vietnam for elementary school students in Vietnam to promote healthy eating habits. The 75-second video describes the risks of eating too much sugar and presents alternative, healthier foods children can choose instead. The research team conducted a lab-in the-field experiment in 12 primary schools in Dong Anh, a peri-urban district outside of Hanoi. At the end of the experiment, children were offered cartons of milk as a thank you gift and could choose between sweetened milk, reduced-sugar milk, and unsweetened milk. Published results from the experiment indicated that the video almost doubled the proportion of children selecting healthier milk. This innovation has potential for scalability and could be easily combined with other habit-forming interventions, such as part of a school-based health curriculum.

description: The original Global Food System Sustainability Index (GFSSI) considered four dimensions of food system sustainability (food security & nutrition, environment, economic and social dimensions) and covered 97 countries from low, middle and high-income regions. One limitation of this index, however, was that the four dimensions were not equally represented, with both the economic and social dimensions depending on a limited number of indicators. In the 2022 paper, CGIAR researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets and their co-author built an extended version of the GFSSI by adding several indicators to the two dimensions where the representativity was weak: the social and economic dimensions. They used the extended GFSSI to investigate whether all four dimensions contribute equally to the change observed in the sustainability of food systems across countries, or whether some dimensions are more important than others, and if so, which dimension(s) and for which (group of) countries.
title: Extended version of the Global Food System Sustainability Index:  a policy relevant tool that can help decision-makers design policies that are more effective

description: Life table data for three native natural enemies of the fall armyworm, namely Cotesia icipe, Chelonus bifoveolatus and Charops diversipes were completed at the five temperature levels 20, 25, 28, 30 and 32 C. In addition, similar studies were concluded with the noctuid pest together with Cotesia marginiventris and Chelonus insularis, two exotic parasitoids newly introduced to Africa for use in biological control campaigns against the fall armyworm. These data are currently used to develop phenology-based simulation models to produce a decision tool to optimize biological control efficiency against the fall armyworm under different climatic and ecological scenarios.

description: The SPaRC model deploys a 'nexus approach' to promoting solar irrigation in groundwater-stressed regions and offers several co-benefits including an additional, counter-climatic income source for farmers, reduction in perverse farm power subsidies, incentive for efficient energy and groundwater use, and reduced GHG emissions from irrigation. In SPaRC, farmers are given financial and institutional assistance to put up solar irrigation pumps that are connected to the grid, with a guaranteed buy-back of any surplus solar electricity. This decentralized grid-connected solar pump approach enables farmers to become "prosumers" of solar energy, increasing their income and resilience by adding solar energy as a "crop." It replaces the need of diesel or electricity in irrigation, helping to reduce GHG emissions. And finally, it also encourages farmers not to use all of their energy for groundwater pumping. This is particularly relevant in groundwater-depleted regions of South Asia, where free or highly subsidized electricity has led to excessive pumping of groundwater. This model creates an opportunity cost of using energy in irrigation, if not sold to the grid. Therefore, with an attractive buyback rate, policymakers can incentivize more efficient use of water and energy.
title: SPaRC model: Grid-connecting solar pumps and buy-back of surplus solar electricity to incentivize efficient energy and water use in Southern Asia

description: The conventional approach to promoting solar irrigation has been through offering subsidies for individual farmers to adopt solar pumps. However, this approach suffers from problems like poor targeting and elite capture, underutilization of created assets and challenges in delivering high quality O&M services. Further, the highly fragmented nature of landholdings render ownership of solar pumps by individual farmers financially and technically infeasible. Another approach has been to support community assets that are owned and operated by user groups. This can improve asset utilization but the problem of underutilization remains; it can also suffer from 'collective action' problems as the responsibility for upkeep of assets gets distributed. With support from IWMI-Tata Program, WLE and CCAFS, IWMI has piloted 'solar irrigation service providers' in Bihar and Jharkhand (India). Likewise, IDCOL - a government owned company in Bangladesh - has supported village-level solar irrigation enterprises on a large scale. As part of its work in Work Package #3, NEXUS Gains will build on this work and support the conceptualization, development, field testing, documentation and scaling of alternate business models for expanding access to solar energy applications for rural livelihoods in eastern Gangetic plains.
title: Catalyzing equitable, sustainable and smallholder-friendly solar energy service markets for enhancing rural livelihoods in Eastern Gangetic Plains

However, in most countries, farmers’ access to quality seed of recently released varieties remains very low. A first stage literature review that will help to define seed delivery pathways for dissemination of new varieties released by CIP in Peru and in other countries. •	Product profiles, market segments, seed delivery pathways / seed business models, and dissemination strategies for new varieties_x000D_
•	Methodologies to estimate seed requirements quantitatively and qualitatively, estimate farmers’ seed demand, and how private companies deal with variability on demand_x000D_
The review will focus on potatoes. Other crops (especially maize) and vegetatively propagated crops (sweetpotato, cassava, banana, and yam) are included for comparative purposes and as relevant.

During the 2021-22 main (wet) season in Mozambique,  a total of fourteen tricot trials were established in ten rice growing hubs (schemes) distributed in five districts. In the off-season, seven released varieties were used for the establishment of eleven tricot trials in Mozambique.

description: The SI-MFS team is developing and piloting an agro advisory tool that will facilitate knowledgeable decision-making by farmers about the best practices in nutrient management. Generated from research-based data integrated with detailed biophysical co-variates, the advisories will also be site- and context-specific. Farmer access to the advisory services will be ensured through customized dissemination channels, including video, Interactive Voice Response, Short Messaging Services, radio, and traditional extension channels. Male and female farmer preferences and constraints will be factored in during the entire process to ensure adaptive learning. The advisory tool will provide site and context advisories for farmers in 3 Woredas during the incubation phase (2023-2024) and upscale to 10 million Maize and Barely growing farmers in Ethiopia until 2030.

description:
The effect of different cutting management on the yield and quality of forage oat and food oat varieties (Desho grass and vetch)  was investigated in Ethiopian Highlands. The oat varieties were harvested at the vegetative and maturity stages to explore if this practice can result in a yield and quality advantage over one-time cutting at maturity. For the forage oat one-time cutting at hay stage was compared with two-time cutting at vegetative and maturity stages. The tree Lucerne cutting management trial plots had been established in the 2021 planting season to generate additional evidence on the optimal cutting height and frequency under field conditions._x000D_
Evidence on forage harvesting frequency and biomass of food-feed oat varieties generated per year will be bundled with other information to promote wider scaling of tree Lucerne in the Ethiopian Highlands.
title: Cutting frequency for  three food-feed oat varieties in crop-livestock mixed systems in Ethiopia

description: Addressing physical and economic water scarcity through the provision of off-grid solar pumps to smallholder farmers in key-value chains and supporting adaption through sustainable finance solutions in Zambia. In many off-grid areas, petrol and diesel pumps are commonly used for irrigation. However, they are expensive to run and contribute to environmental pollution. With the abundance of sunshine in Sub Sahara Africa, solar pumps offer small farmers a promising alternative – if they can afford the initial investment. Financial mechanisms like pay-as-you-go models are linked to asset sales to decrease the investment threshhold for smallhold farmers.
title: Providing off-grid solar irrigation technologies and services to low-income farmers through inclusive and sustainable end-user finance mechanisms.

description: The doubled-up legume system involving groundnuts and pigeon pea, comes across as being a perfect combination as the groundnuts only exploit the shallow soil profile and mature relatively faster whereas pigeon peas develop much slower while being deeper-rooted, leading to less competition in the system. Pigeon peas mature at least 2-3 months after the groundnuts, usually providing an increase in overall grain yield from both crops. Pigeon peas also add a large amount of slow decomposing biomass, besides nitrogen rich leaves and stems, which can be used partially as surface mulch or firewood. This benefits the whole cropping system and the household.
title: In doubled-up legume systems several legumes are strategically combined in the same planting space. Doubled legume systems are a principle of sustainable intensification to increase crop yields per unit land area.

description: The AgWise modular decision support framework consists of sequential crop modeling and machine learning steps that use public data on weather and soils, and a variety of agronomic trial data to generate recommendations that can increase yields and profit for farmers. It was created via agreement among data scientists across Centers to support EiA use case analytics and advisory goals. However, AgWise is intended to be "use case agnostic", and thus generalizable to any Use Case and  agronomy recommendation needs of external partners beyond the life of this initiative. The framework includes the logic, work modalities, workflows, data sourcing methodologies, scripts and repositories (with CG Labs as a collaborative workbench), initially focused on generating fertilizer and planting date recommendations for several crops in different agroecologies.

description: The Collaborative GARDIAN (CG) Labs high-performance compute-and-store solution was improved through targeted development to maximize cost efficiency to advance data science for agriculture, particularly in limited bandwidth situations. This infrastructure works more or less like a supercomputer cluster, but is optimized for low bandwidth environments. An authenticated user (typically a data scientist) can choose a high, medium, or low computing environment based on their needs, and CG Labs will spin up a virtual machine for them/their teams to proceed with setting up particular large data sources, analytics jobs etc. This innovation is being improved through use and feedback from other initiatives and non-pooled projects.

description: This toolkit will form an accessible and easily understandable 'checklist' based toolkit containing practical and actionable guidelines for the design of climate security-sensitive livestock sector-specific adaptation and mitigation policies. Previous research has demonstrated that awareness of climate-related security risks in key climate-related policy outputs across ClimBeR countries is limited, despite the increasing salience of pursuing adaptation and mitigation in fragile and conflict-affected areas. The toolkit will likely focus on both conceptual considerations (appropriate conceptualisations of climate security) and on technical considerations (inclusion and deployment of certain types of analyses and features of policy design). The toolkit will be aimed at policymakers, technical ministerial staff, and supporting entities in the governance space.
title: Livestock 4 Climate Security Policy and Governance Toolkit: Ensuring Climate Security-sensitive and Pro-peace Livestock Adaptation and Mitigation. A toolkit which will contain recommendations on how to mainstream climate security in relevant policies for policy makers

description: Varietal resistance against Fusarium Head Blight (FHB) is incomplete and is subject to environmental conditions and pathogenic variation; thus an integrated disease management package involving resistant germplasm, fungicide application, cultural control methods etc. is often indispensable. Under the Plant Health Initiative (PHI), in 2022, we evaluated a set of wheat genotypes with resistance to wheat blast in field experiments in Mexico and Zambia along with different fungicide ingredients, application timing, and spray nozzles, to identify the best management approach under smallholders' wheat cropping systems in the local environments. Final results will be available in 2023.
title: Integrated disease management of Fusarium Head Blight (FHB) in the smallholders' cropping systems in Mexico and Zambia

description: The wheat blast caused by a fungal pathogen, Magnaporthe oryzae Triticum (MoT) pathotype, was detected in Bangladesh for the first time in 2016 and 2019 in Zambia. The disease is expanding in these countries and threatening to spread to neighboring regions. An early warning system for the wheat blast is very important for informing farmers about the blast risk so that management actions like fungicide application can be done in a timely manner. The wheat blast early warning system has been developed in Bangladesh, and the prototype is validated for its suitability for early warning advisory to farmers for effective management of the disease. The same model will be validated in Zambia and promoted in both countries to benefit more farmers.
title: Wheat Blast Early Warning System model for supporting farmers and enabling timely decision-making in Zambia and Bangladesh

description: A protocol for improved understanding of how integrating men’s engagement on involvement in household chores and childcare activities into a social protection graduation model program can affect men’s behaviors and gender attitudes. As learning partners for the Strengthening PSNP for Institutions and Resilience (SPIR) program that provides gender-sensitive livelihood and nutrition programming in a graduation model to beneficiary households in Ethiopia’s Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), IFPRI researchers are collaborating with implementation partners from World Vision, CARE and the Organization for Rehabilitation and Development in Amhara (ORDA) to design and implement an experimental impact evaluation to test the effectiveness of a men’s engagement training to encourage men to reconsider their roles in support of household chores and childcare activities. The study uses reporting from both men and their female partners on men’s behaviors on these tasks and examines whether changes in men’s behaviors are accompanied with changes in gender attitudes.

description: This innovation is a novel approach to measuring impacts of social protection programs, in terms of their roles in supporting gendered responses to climate change in low- and middle-income countries. A multi-disciplinary team of researchers have designed a protocol that includes combining data from an experimental impact evaluation of a social protection program with detailed weather data from satellites to investigate how the social protection programs shape gender dimensions of outcomes from extreme weather events. The data for this research is drawn from country-specific sources on weather events and nationally or locally implemented social protection programs.
title: Study protocols for country-specific analysis of climate data combined with existing data on women’s well-being from randomized impact evaluations of social protection programs

description: This framework conceptualizes how social protection can shape the effect of climate change on women and girls’ well-being. The conceptual framework highlights a set of pathways whereby social safety nets, by building household and women’s resilience capacities, can improve how women, households, and communities respond to climate change. This framework will be used to summarize the existing evidence on how social protection leads to improved and inclusive responses to climate change, and where knowledge gaps may exist.

description: A pre-registration is a time-stamped research plan that researchers can create and upload before conducting a study. The objective of pre-registration is to provide researchers with an overview of ongoing studies in their field and to build research transparency by reducing selective reporting. While pre-registration is commonplace for clinical health trials, its use in development economics is more recent, and WP3 decided to adopt this latest standard for their field experiments. This particular experiment by IFPRI, Wageningen University, ACRE Africa, and the Kenyan Agriculture and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) in Kenya will test the effects of providing trial packs versus a consumer-oriented intervention (which is still being finalized) on varietal adoption by smallholder farmers. Effects of trial packs will be compared with the effects of providing remote personalized advisories, and insurance subsidies.
title: Registration of the Trial “Testing what works to accelerate varietal turnover: An experiment in Kenya”

description: The Impacts Dashboard for Genetic Innovation was internally launched within CGIAR Genetic Innovation to assist researchers, managers and investors in visualizing Impact Opportunities and prioritizing Seed Product Market Segments (SPMS). The current version 2.0 features 93 indicators of Impact Opportunities across the five Impact Areas (Nutrition, Health and Food Security; Poverty Reduction, Livelihoods and Jobs; Gender Equality, Youth and Inclusion; Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation; and Environmental Health and Biodiversity) and a cross-cutting category. It features two filters that enable researchers identifying global Impact Opportunities for prioritization at three levels: (1) globally, (2) based on all CGIAR SPMS (Market Segment Footprint), and (3) based on all active CGIAR SPMS that are currently served by Breeding Pipelines. Prioritization can be conducted at seven aggregate levels: (1) CGIAR Regions, (2) CGIAR Sub-regions, (3) Centers, (4) Crops, (5) Breeding Pipelines, (6) SPMS, and (7) Countries. Impact Opportunities are downscaled from national to SPMS levels using Impact Area-specific scaling methods (e.g., based on targeted area, targeted calories produced, targeted production value, share of agricultural GDP, crop-specific greenhouse gas emissions, and crop-specific global genebank accessions). Users can visualize priorities at the three levels for all seven aggregates in three ways: (1) based on a single indicator through a treemap and (2) a global map, or (3) based on multiple indicators through two area charts, one for breadth indicators and another one for incidence indicators. The Impacts Dashboard for Genetic Innovation v2.0 is a prototype that will be integrated into the Global Market Intelligence Platform in 2023, which is one of the core innovations of the CGIAR Initiative on Market Intelligence.

description: Created with CCAFS West Africa support in 2012, the national science-policy dialogue platform in Mali (C-CASA Mali) has promoted consultation between researchers-public authorities-NGOs-farmers' organizations-grassroots actors, thus have been crucial to improve interactions between policy makers and researchers. Member-institutions adherence and participation to the platform's vision and activities are key factors determining the platform's ability to play its part in climate governance in Mali. The platform's institutionalization and the stakeholders' commitment have enabled the platform to play a key role in the identification and prioritization of climate-smart agriculture practices and investment portfolios. The knowledge generated by the platform through its research made it possible to identify constraints and challenges, to inform and guide adaptation planning and governance in Malian agriculture/food systems. The establishment of platforms at district level is necessary to consider the concerns of grassroots communities and a better harmonization in the implementation of climate change adaptation programs and policies.

description: Supplementing increasing levels of dried tagasaste (Chamaecytisus palmensis) leaf on the nutrition and performance of sheep feed. Research shows intake and digestibility of dry matter and nutrients will increase as tagasaste supplementation increase from 100 to 400 g/day. Average body weight gain will increase from 20 to 73 g/day, feed conversion efficiency from 0.04 to 0.10, dressing percentage from 40 to 48. As the supplementation increase from 100 to 400 g/day. Proportion of tagasaste leaf in the diet will increase from 20 to 50%, while the ratio of neutral detergent fibre to crude protein will be decreased from 7.9 to 5.3, as the level of supplementation increased. Supplementation of dried tagasaste leaf up to 50% of the diet DM, resulting in an NDF:CP ratio of 5.3, produces no deleterious effects on sheep, and inclusion to this level can be applied for superior growth performance and carcass yield in sheep diets.

description: Addressing malnutrition and poor soils requires diversification. Production of protein-rich grains from legumes addresses the problem of poor access to foods that contribute to healthy diets. Traditionally, farmers in Malawi lakeshore zone have gown maize and cowpea in a relay intercropping system, using spreading cowpea landraces. In this system, maize is planted at the onset of rains, normally during December, and cowpea is then relay introduced during March, when the maize crop will be towards physiological maturity. Maize is then harvested a month later, having barely suffered from intra specific competition for water, nutrients and light from the young cowpea plants.  Cowpea then continues growth as a sole crop, mostly using residual moisture as rainfall within the lakeshore zone often tail off during April.

description:
Knowledge Platform for Inclusive and Sustainable Food Markets and Value Chains (KISM) is a platform to help farmer organizations, food businesses, governments, and practitioners make better-informed investment and policy decisions on inclusive and sustainable food value chains. The platform consolidates available evidence of existing experiences with product and process innovations within food value chains regarding their impact in terms of inclusiveness (employment and income generation, value-added sharing, poverty reduction, food security) and sustainability (emissions, supply chain resilience). _x000D_
Users can access the knowledge platform through a dedicated website. Available evidence on the effectiveness of (bundled) value chain innovations is presented by using the logic of the Initiative's theory of change (ToC). Users can further access various tools for value chain analysis, including the Tools4VCs set developed previously by CGIAR's research program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (PIM). Furthermore, through the platform users can connect with other communities of practice (CoP), including the "Living Income CoP". KISM has further been designed to undertake e-disussions and serve as a hub for policy and stakeholder dialogues undertaken by the Initiative.

description: The Livestock and Climate Initiative has strengthened governance, management and restoration of rangelands in two conservancies (Irong and Paka), one community forest (Koitegan) and one unregistered rangeland (Kabarion) in Baringo county, Kenya. This covers a total of 91,390 hectares. This has resulted in reduced land use conflicts and communities better placed to protect their lands from encroachment. Land tenure security had incentivized communities to improve livestock production working with ILRI to livestock breeds and mobilising their own resources to undertake rangeland restoration as well as support rangeland restoration trials. Women’s involvement in decision making processes has increased aided by building women’s confidence through community conversations. These successes have been recognized by the county government who included participatory rangeland management in their county integrated development plan.

description: The Livestock and Climate Initiative has strengthened governance, management and restoration of 165,326 hectares of shared grazing lands in four clusters of villages in Kiteto district, Manyara region, Tanzania through joint village land use planning and participatory rangeland management. This has resulted in reduced land use conflicts for the four livestock keeper associations and the residents in the area, who are better placed to protect their lands from encroachment. Land tenure security had incentivized communities to improve livestock production through buying improved breeds and mobilising their own resources to undertake rangeland restoration on 162 hectares of land. Women’s involvement in decision making processes has increased aided by building women’s confidence through women’s leadership forums. These successes have been recognized by national government, including the uptaking of joint village land use planning into national guidelines.

description: Community conversations can support locally led adaptation and are a method of engaging communities to address development and social issues based on their identification of priorities and actions. Community conversations were implemented in two villages in Baringo County, Kenya to support locally led equitable adaptation, whereby local people identified key activities to increase adaptation capacities of women, men and youth. Baseline findings showed that adaptation capacities were relatively low and that norms restricted women’s participation in decision-making, time use and movement. A total of 4 conversations involving 1,325 farmers and agropastoralists were held over one year. Interactive and participatory methods included drama, a radio show, and technical training to enhance livestock production. Analysis of midline quantitative and qualitative data showed significant changes in women’s and men’s beliefs in both communities around livestock ownership, selling and, among other areas, women’s mobility.
title: CGIAR innovation community conversations contributes to positive change in transforming attitudes towards gender equity

description: In Tanzania policy and legislation provides for the provision of certificates of customary rights of occupancy (CCROs). However commonly these are issued on an individual basis and challenges arise when trying to secure tenure for a group that shares resources. The Livestock and Climate Initiative has been working with the Government of Tanzania to pilot the provision of group CCROs to livestock keeper associations. In late 2024 a group CCRO was issued to the Amei village livestock keepers association to secure 50,588 hectares of shared grazing land benefiting 15,407 livestock keepers predominantly pastoralists. Amei is part of the four village cluster of villages making up the ALOLLE shared grazing land.

description: Kenya Integrated Agricultural Management Information System (KIAMIS) leverages the KAZNET platform, developed by ILRI and supported by the Livestock and Climate Initiative to deliver real-time livestock market intelligence, to enhance decision-making and resilience among Kenya’s pastoralists. Through KAZNET, data on market prices, traded volumes, livestock quality, and household coping strategies are collected by 51 citizen contributors across Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands. This information is disseminated directly to 1,010 pastoralists through pastoralist groups and indirectly reaches another 2,979 pastoralists belonging to 270 pastoralist groups in Kenya. This information is crucial for empowering pastoralists with actionable insights to optimize livestock trade and resource management. KIAMIS’s integration of KAZNET represents a significant step in institutionalizing market intelligence within public systems, ensuring accessibility and transparency for both pastoralists and policymakers. The geo-referenced data collection system and innovative use of photo validation enhance the accuracy and reliability of market data.

description: Hacienda San José (HSJ) demonstrates the remarkable ecological benefits of maintaining buffer zones around riparian forests and connectivity corridors in the Orinoquia region of Colombia. These buffer zones, spanning 200 meters and preserved from cattle grazing and annual burning for over seven years, provide critical habitat for bird biodiversity, offering refuge and resources for diverse avian species. The undisturbed native savanna vegetation within the 200-meter-wide and 3–4-kilometer-long connectivity areas enhances carbon sequestration, contributing significantly to carbon stocks by maintaining soil health and vegetation cover. Additionally, these zones promote natural connectivity, enabling the movement of wildlife and the regeneration of native flora, which are vital for ecosystem resilience. By integrating these conservation practices, HSJ fosters sustainable land management, contrasting sharply with the degradation caused by uncontrolled grazing and burning in the region. This approach highlights the multifaceted benefits of buffer zones for biodiversity, carbon storage, and long-term environmental sustainability.
title: Buffer zones developed by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT are being used by Hacienda San Jose, Colombia

description: Joint village land use planning was developed to address the challenges of protecting and facilitating the sharing of natural resources across village administrative boundaries. Supported by enabling policy and legislation it enables villages sharing a grazing land, water point, forest or conservation area to develop a joint village land use agreement. This agreement protects the use of the land (no village can change the use without approval of all villages and is the foundation of secure collective resource rights through the issuing of certificates of customary rights of occupancy. Piloted, implemented and being scaled by the Livestock and Climate Initiative working closely with the Government of Tanzania, in 2024 it facilitated the securing of 2,365 hectares of shared grazing lands for 10,167 (5,527 female and 4,640 male) livestock keepers from four villages - Kimange, Miono, Mkwajuni and Kweikonje villages, Chalinze District, Coastal region, Tanzania

description: The Government of Ethiopia, namely the Ministry of Irrigation and Lowlands has committed to investing US$52.5 million of a US$340 million World Bank soft loan Lowlands Livelihoods Resilience Project (Phase II) to the updating of the 28 existing rangeland management investment plans prepared under the first phase and the formulation of new rangeland management plans through participatory rangeland management principles to identify additional climate-smart mitigation and nature-based solutions, validate their feasibility based on indicative land-use planning and characterization and formulate rangeland management bylaws (page 9 in World Bank Project Appraisal Document). Their point of reference is the Introductory Guidelines on Participatory Rangeland Management produced by ILRI Senior Scientist Fiona Flintan. Participatory rangeland management is a community-led process facilitated by practitioners to build community capacities to better manage, govern and restore their lands. It is anticipated that ILRI will provide technical support to this application.

description: Through collaborative research and action, ICARDA and the Tunisian government have pioneered opportunistic grazing as an innovative approach to sustainable rangeland management within the Sustainable Rangeland Management toolkit, guided by scientific principles and enriched by local knowledge. Opportunistic grazing involves allowing livestock to graze on available forage during favorable conditions, ensuring optimal resource utilization. By adopting this approach, rangeland managers can maximize forage use, enhance ecosystem health, and achieve livestock production goals. Pastoralists in the Al Mustakbal "Future" Agricultural Development group located in Douz, south Tunisia have optaken opportunistic grazing across 50,000 hectares of rangelands benefiting 1,250 pastoralists.

description: This report summarizes a qualitative evaluation by the MELIA team on Kenya’s Living Labs for People (LL4P), implemented in Nandi County by the Mitigate+ Initiative. LL4P provides a space for stakeholders to co-design, test, and advance socio-technical innovations for sustainable food systems with mitigation benefits. Key users include farmers, organizations, and local governments. The evaluation found that LL4P successfully established an inclusive, co-owned, and autonomous framework. Researchers identified the Kaimosi Agricultural Training Center (KATC) as a local host and secured stakeholder commitment. While the Initiative facilitated the process, stakeholders have taken the lead. LL4P now operates independently with a diverse nine-member board, including four women, one youth, and six farmers.

description: The CGIAR-supported innovation Index-Based Livestock Insurance is a risk-mitigating tool that encourages livestock keepers to insure their livestock against loss in times of drought or other crises. Facilitated by private sector insurance companies, this insurance provides payouts triggered by satellite-monitored vegetation data, reducing the financial burden of livestock losses caused by forage scarcity. Since 2012 ILRI has been developing IBLI with insurance companies gradually extending its reach. Since 2022-3 its accessibility has been significantly increased to pastoralists Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia with support from a new World Bank project - De-risking, Inclusion and Value Enhancement- and uptake through Zep-Re Insurance company predicting reach to 250,000 pastoralists in five years.
title: Zep-Re insurance company increases reach of CGIAR innovation Index-based Livestock Insurance to predicted 250,000 pastoralists in Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia in five years

description: The Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform, supported by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, leverages the KAZNET platform, developed by ILRI and supported by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate, to enhance its capacity for monitoring rangeland conditions, livestock markets, and household coping strategies across five arid and semi-arid counties: Marsabit, Samburu, Isiolo, Garissa, and Wajir. By integrating data from 'citizen contributors' and 'super contributors' trained to gather and validate market and environmental information, Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform provides real-time, geo-referenced insights essential for decision-making in drought-prone areas. The platform empowers public institutions to deliver timely, data-driven interventions, addressing critical gaps in livestock market intelligence and rangeland management. This collaboration ensures actionable climate and livestock information reaches policymakers, pastoralists, and other stakeholders, fostering resilience in Kenya’s drylands. KAZNET's integration within the Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform underscores the importance of participatory and digital solutions in transforming livestock production systems.

description: The government Office de l'Elevage et du Paturage (OEP), Tunisia has uptaken CGIAR innovation CLEANED to promote sustainable livestock practices in the country. With support from the Livestock and Climate Initiative and GIZ the tool has been integrated into projects aimed at reducing the environmental footprint of livestock systems (particularly dairy) while improving productivity and livelihoods. The tool has been used to assess the impact of livestock on water, land and greenhouse gas emissions, raising awareness of policymakers to the climate impacts of their livestock sector and options for mitigation. On-demand trainings on CLEANED were provided enabling OEP to use CLEANED for scenario analysis and decision-making. The OEP and others undertook a national survey of dairy farms using the CLEANED concrete assessment. This contributes to Tunisia's national objectives and efforts to meet its Paris Agreement climate commitments by improving data collection, availability and assessment through tools such as CLEANED.

description: CLEANED (Comprehensive livestock environmental assessment for improved nutrition, a secured environment and sustainable development along livestock value chains), is a multi-dimensional modelling tool designed to produce rapid environmental impact assessments in mixed crop-livestock farming systems in developing countries. Improved over the last three years it can be used at the livestock production level as well as guiding policy decisions and public and private sector investments towards more sustainable livestock production. With support from the Livestock and Climate Initiative in collaboration with the Sustainable Animal Productivity Initiative, CLEANED is now being used in three new countries (Colombia, Ecuador and Peru) with further training and assessments carried out in Tunisia, Colombia and Peru. A user survey confirms user benefits.

description: Developed by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate together with partners as an approach to social learning and scaling, Pioneer Positive Deviance enables more than 15,424 pioneer households in livestock management in Kenya to access climate-smart livestock practices through farmer2farmer networks. 39 pioneer households have engaged 4,400 participants across 37 field days. Additionally, 23,000 booklets on feed management for dairy, co-designed with these pioneer households, have been distributed in collaboration with 16 network partners. An assessment of the approach at site level highlights the effectiveness of this approach, showing high adoption rates of climate-smart livestock practices e.g. improved forage and feed. Respondents reported significant improvements in livestock productivity after adopting the pioneer-developed practices, including increased milk production (75.8%), better livestock health (52.5%), and enhanced cost efficiency (29.9%). Furthermore, 80% of survey participants actively share knowledge with other, primarily with neighbors and friends, leveraging social networks to expand impact.

description: Developed by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate together with partners as an approach to social learning and scaling, Pioneer Positive Deviance identifies innovative farmer-led solutions developed by pioneer households in response to climate-related challenges in livestock management. The solutions are shared through farmer2farmer networks and field days for scaling within and beyond  communities. In Kenya it has enabled 45 pioneer households in Bomet and Nandi counties to share innovations and is being adopted by the county extension systems. In Ethiopia, it was piloted in Amhara region with 40 pioneer households invested in sheep fattening. Though security issues prevented full implementation 13,752 co-designed booklets on sheep fattening were distributed in 36 villages. Stakeholder workshops led three universities to incorporate Pioneer Positive Deviance, with plans to expand its use in the national extension system. These efforts showcase its potential to drive farmer-led innovation and inclusive scaling across diverse contexts.

description: This initiative supports vulnerable communities in Kenya and Uganda by enhancing climate resilience through sustainable agricultural practices, improved water and resource management, and climate-smart technologies. By providing technical assistance, policy alignment, and stakeholder engagement, CGIAR ClimBeR has supported the development of robust Green Climate Fund (GCF) proposals in Uganda (in collaboration with IUCN) and Kenya (in collaboration with AGNES). These proposals address local needs, integrate cross-border cooperation, and foster inclusive participation, focusing on gender, youth, and marginalized groups. Moreover, ClimBeR’s expertise in aligning county-level adaptation plans with national objectives and leveraging local knowledge has been pivotal in ensuring context-specific, effective, and impactful interventions for climate resilience and food security.

description:
IRRI partnering with the NARES had developed local service providers (LSP) involving women and youth in harvesting paddy by using a reaper. A total of four couples service providers harvested 35 hectares of land in 2024. Among them two pairs of service providers embarked on their entrepreneurial journey back in 2020. They established different business models using their incomes. The most notable business was the establishment of grocery shop, rearing milking cows, fish farming in homestead pond and purchasing new reapers via the government’s subsidized agricultural mechanization promotion program. _x000D_
_x000D_
In 2024, the service providers used their earnings for several key areas, including the purchasing agricultural land, procurement of grocery items for household consumption and grocery store, purchased agricultural inputs and livestock feed, invest on children's education, repairing agricultural machineries (mostly reaper) and some funds also set aside for family healthcare

description: In India, the Vision-to-action and co-design process led to the development and implementation of agroecological practices including: Microsite (Krishi kund) for restoration of degraded land, Integrated Farming System (IFS) models, and installation of Solar Irrigation pumps with women led Water User Groups (WUG). In Mandla, 16 farmers adopted Microsite (Krishi kund) to restore their degraded land and increased their productivity by 2.39 to 5.71 times. A total of 15 farmers adopted Integrated Farming System (IFS) models, resulting in higher productivity, increased income, improved soil biodiversity, increased insect diversity and earthworm populations. Installation of solar irrigation pumps and formation of women-led water user groups benefitted 27 farmers by enabling regular supply of water for crop diversification and crop cultivation throughout the year. In Andhra Pradesh, 22 farmers participated in Rice-Fish based field experimentation with Mola fish, contributing to the development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for managing Rice-Fish system under natural farming. More farmers have shown interest, participated in training programs, and begun adopting agroecological practices, including partial implementation of the models.
title: In India, 80 farmers engaged the Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALL) in Madhya and Andhra Pradesh adopt codeveloped agroecological practices, resulting in crop diversification, increased income, productivity and biodiversity.

description: Farmerline, a social enterprise operating in Ghana, utilizes the Multi-Dimensional Inclusivity Index (MDII) to assess and enhance the inclusivity of its Business-to-Farmer (B2F) services. The evaluation revealed that Farmerline’s digital solutions, including its call center and matchmaking services, are highly accessible and beneficial, providing smallholder farmers with advisory services, financial support, and market linkages. However, gaps were identified in co-creation, training, and support, particularly for elderly and illiterate farmers. Based on the MDII findings, Farmerline committed to improving inclusivity by strengthening farmer participation in service design, expanding training programs for marginalized users, and refining its digital tools for broader accessibility. Additionally, the assessment informed strategies to mitigate risks such as digital exclusion and environmental impacts.

description:
Farmers in the solar groundwater trial now have reliable water sources, reducing time spent fetching water, especially for young girls. They also grow vegetables during the rice off-season for consumption and sale, improving their diet. The trial established one wetland management committee, four production groups, and four Water User Groups. Farmers were trained and groundwater wells were built in four villages, each with solar-powered pumps, water tanks, and monitoring systems.  _x000D_
Key Outcomes:_x000D_
- Environmental: Wells addressed climate variability, supporting rainfed agriculture during droughts.  _x000D_
- Social: Reliable water access improved domestic use and irrigation, reducing the burden on women and strengthening community governance.  _x000D_
- Economic: Solar-powered systems eliminated electricity costs, providing a cost-effective solution. Year-round vegetable farming enhanced food security and economic stability.

description: The Virtual Irrigation Academy (VIA) utilizes the Multi-Dimensional Inclusivity Index (MDII), developed by Digital Innovation, to assess the social inclusivity of its Chameleon Water Sensor (CWS) in South Africa and Malawi. The MDII evaluates digital innovations across five key dimensions—access, usability, benefits, participation, and consequences—ensuring that the CWS remains accessible, relevant, and beneficial to smallholder farmers. The assessment revealed that while the CWS is widely accessible and effective, barriers such as limited internet access for Wi-Fi-enabled features and affordability constraints exist. VIA used the findings to enhance inclusivity, improve engagement with farmers, and refine the MDII tool itself. The review also demonstrated the value of the CWS to external partners and funding agencies, reinforcing VIA’s commitment to making its technology socially inclusive and beneficial for marginalized communities.

description: An innovation challenge and hackathon was organized to tackle two critical issues: inefficient organic waste management in the agri-food sector and the lack of technological innovation in waste utilization processes. The initiative aimed to foster innovative solutions from students, focusing on optimizing organic waste use through black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens). A total of 70 students—64 from SENA's CDTI and 6 from the Universidad Autónoma de Occidente—participated in the challenge, which unfolded in three phases. Their mission was to design and develop an automated production unit for converting organic waste into valuable resources using black soldier fly larvae. Students worked in multidisciplinary teams to design and prototype the production units during the three phases of the challenge. This initiative empowered students to apply technology and sustainability principles, driving forward a more efficient and eco-friendly approach to waste management.

description: In Tunisia ICARDA developed a technology and scaling methodology for a more resilient, low-emission livestock feed system to alleviate pressure on grazing lands with the support from Livestock and Climate and the Initiative on Agroecology. The system uses a small-scale compressor that produces pellets from nutritious agricultural byproducts. After refining the formula with farmers using locally available inputs, scaling focused on farmer cooperatives in the south of Tunisia, where there is high demand for supplementary feeds. A private-public partnership was established with the national government Office de l’Elevage et des Pâturages and private sector partner Juhaina to facilitate this scaling. Trainings and demonstrations were co-organised to show farmers the advantages and how to use the pelleting machine. Over 60 machines have now been sold with 100s of livestock keepers benefiting whilst alleviating pressure on grazing areas. The system is now being shared in other countries to encourage uptake.

description:
The livestock feed sector in Uganda is mostly controlled by small-scale companies who offer costly, inadequate feeds, leaving farmers with few choices. The rise of small-scale feed producers has transformed concentrate feed production, offering opportunities while simultaneously presenting challenges such as insufficient technical expertise in feed formulation and mixing, resulting in the manufacture of costly and substandard feeds._x000D_
_x000D_
An intervention was implemented by SAPLING with 40 feed producers in two phases across the project districts. In the first phase, the feed producers were trained in principles of feed formulation. In the second phase, the trained feed producers were mentored on good feed manufacturing practices (GMP) for feed production for 8 months. They were assessed for their adherence to the procedures they had learned. The results indicate that in addition to those who were already following certain GMPs, a larger number of feed producers are now compliant with most of the practices.
title: Adoption of good manufacturing practices by small scale feed producers in Uganda through SAPLING supported trainings

description: Food, land and water (FLW) systems face challenges from a host of interacting megatrends as well as local and regional drivers such as changes in population, urbanization, income, inequality, migration, diets, technology, biodiversity, and climate. Many of these trends are themselves influenced by changes in FLW systems, interacting in complex ways that have important impacts on nutrition, poverty, equity, climate, and  environment.  To capture these complexities we need among other things quantitative tools that help us understand how, where and at what cost these complex  interactions are manifest across the food system at global and regional scales.  This innovation draws on CGIAR’s biophysical and socioeconomic expertise to enhance the IMPACT model by developing and enhancing specific modules to better understand FLW system outcomes under plausible future scenarios. Testing of scenarios in IMPACT was done through engagement with researchers from CG Centers, national agricultural research systems and national government in LMICs.

description: Prior to 2022, smallholder farmers in Kiambu relied heavily on inorganic fertilizers and pesticides, believing organic alternatives were ineffective and unavailable. The Agroecology Initiative WP3 introduced farmer training through a Training of Trainers (ToT) model, training 45 ToTs on agroecological pest control and organic fertilizer production, particularly vermicompost using red worms. Partnering with Comfort Worms and Insects Ltd, the Initiative developed an outgrower scheme, training 10 farmers to produce vermicompost and sell it to the company. Additionally, farmers with access to animal manure supplied it for processing, receiving 30% of the finished product in return. These approaches increased vermicompost production from one to four tonnes per week. Initially, less than 10% of vermicompost was used locally, but with increased production and training, over 25% is now adopted by smallholder farmers, improving soil health and sustainability in Kiambu ALL.

description: Around 1,000 South African youth are tackling environmental challenges through the Enviro-Champs initiative, combining citizen science and digital innovation to drive sustainable change. Originating in Mpophomeni township, KwaZulu-Natal, the program, supported by the Duzi-uMngeni Conservation Trust (DUCT), has expanded with government investment to address water leaks, waste management, and flood preparedness. Through a partnership with the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), the Digital Innovation Initiative empowers young people through UNICEF Impact Youth Market (YOMA) platform with green "learning to earning" opportunities, enhancing their skills in environmental monitoring. The partnership integrates digital tools like Open Data Kit (ODK) to improve data collection and decision-making for water management in the Limpopo Basin. By valuing indigenous knowledge, action-learning, and capacity building, Enviro-Champs not only contribute to ecological restoration but also gain vital skills, employment, and economic empowerment, bridging the digital divide while promoting sustainable development.

description: The Association for Water and Rural Development (AWARD), a South Africa-based nonprofit organization, provides technical support to the Inkomati-Usuthu Catchment Management Agency (IUCMA). The AWARD team proposed that IUCMA integrate Digital Innovation's dynamic water quality monitoring tool, FishTrac is a digital innovation in water quality monitoring that utilizes real-time tracking of fish behavior to assess aquatic ecosystem health, into its water resource management system, the Integrated Water Resource Decision Support System (INWARDs). This integration not only enhances INWARDs' existing dashboards but also fosters opportunities for future collaboration. The shared infrastructure between FishTrac and INWARDs, supported by the IWMI's Digital Twin Application Programming Interface, strengthens data-sharing capabilities across platforms such as the Limpopo Information Management System (LIMIS) and has the potential to contribute to broader transboundary water management initiatives.

description: An agronomic assessment by the Initiative reveals that crop associations have proven highly beneficial across various countries. A trial in Fatick, Senegal, conducted by ISRA, CIRAD, and ENDA, demonstrated that millet grain productivity increased 30-times and the biomass four times when grown after groundnut and cowpea rotation, compared to millet grown without the legume’s rotation. Similarly, CIMMYT, government agencies, and development partners, in collaboration with local communities, implemented push-pull intercropping systems of maize or sorghum with beans or cowpea, reducing fall armyworm damage by 22%. In India, multilayer cropping systems boosted income and food security, while rice-legume rotations in Lao PDR are looking to enhance soil fertility. These examples underscore the versatile roles crop associations play in improving productivity, resilience, and sustainability. By using synergies among crops, agroecological systems can address critical challenges such as pest management, soil health, and food security, making them vital for sustainable agricultural landscapes.

description: Access to Climate Information Services (CIS) in Senegal has significantly improved in recent years, playing a crucial role in enhancing resilience and adaptation to climate variability, particularly for farmers, pastoralists communities. ClimBeR in collaboration with ANACIM (Met service) has been instrumental in generating and disseminating timely weather forecasts, early warnings, and agro-climatic advisories. These services are delivered through multiple channels, including SMS, Interactive Voice Response (IVR), community radios, mobile applications, ensuring that climate information reaches diverse user groups. Despite these advancements, challenges remain, particularly in last-mile delivery to remote rural areas, gender-inclusive access, and ensuring that the information is actionable and tailored to local needs. Strengthening partnerships between meteorological agencies, research institutions, and digital innovation platforms can further enhance the accessibility, usability, and impact of climate information services, ultimately supporting informed decision-making and climate resilience in Senegal’s agriculture and food systems.

description: An agronomic assessment undertaken by the Initiative assessed agroecological innovations in India and Laos, co-designed by IWMI, partners, and local communities, aimed at diversifying traditional paddy rice monocropping systems. In India, 46% of households adopting multilayer crop systems on small plots (approximately 1000 m²) experienced increased income compared to rice cultivation on the same area. These systems, integrating up to 15 crops, were implemented by women self-help groups from tribal communities with support from PRADAN, targeting enhanced income and improved nutrition. In Laos, as part of an integrated wetland management approach, rice-fish culture is being promoted to further diversify paddy rice systems. These efforts collectively seek to strengthen food security, provide year-round income, and reduce reliance on rice monoculture while fostering agroecological practices.

Established in response to farmer demand, the plant—operated by community-selected members—has provided an affordable, sustainable alternative to conventional animal feed. description: In Tunisia, ICARDA and INRAT led research to improve soil health and plant productivity in the semi-arid El Kef-Siliana transect. as revealed by an agronomic assessment of the Initiative, Rhizobium inoculation significantly enhanced biomass production in both durum wheat and the melliferous fodder sulla plant. In sulla, inoculation doubled plant height and boosted biomass to over 7.5 tons/ha, compared to 3.8 tons/ha for non-inoculated plants. Similarly, inoculation in durum wheat doubled biomass, which is used as a high-protein fodder crop under semi-arid conditions. Additionally, combining biochar with chemical fertilizers nearly doubled durum wheat grain yield compared to treatments without biochar, highlighting biochar’s role in optimizing fertilizer efficiency. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating rhizobium inoculation and biochar to enhance soil health, improve biomass, and maximize grain production, offering a sustainable approach to farming in semi-arid regions undergoing agroecological transition. In this regard, in Zimbabwe biochar is also being tested in maize and sorghum.

description: The agronomic assessment done by the Agroecology Initiative revealed: Trials in organic cacao orchards at the Pucallpa ALL in Peru, co-designed by the Alliance Bioversity & CIAT with the Colpa de Loros and Banaqui-Curimana cooperatives, highlighted the vital role of cultural practices in managing cacao fruit diseases. Regularly harvesting diseased fruits proved the most effective strategy, keeping moniliasis incidences below 5% in well-managed orchards, compared to nearly five times higher in orchards neglecting this practice, regardless of biofungicide use. These findings underscore the agroecological value of reducing disease pressure through simple, low-cost practices rather than relying solely on external inputs. Although unusually warm and dry conditions during the 2023–2024 season contributed to low disease levels, the trials demonstrated that cultural practices could safeguard production even in favorable conditions for disease suppression. This evidence underscores the need to prioritize cultural practices as key components of sustainable and agroecological disease management in cacao production systems.

description: The Circular Bioeconomy Innovation Hub in Ghana is a multistakeholder platform initiated by IWMI as one-stop-shop for training, research, advisory support, collaboration and knowledge sharing. The hub unites now 17 stakeholders from the public and private sectors, research institutions, non-governmental organizations, and education to promote circular bioeconomy initiatives. Operating in the organic waste-to-resource value chain, a co-ownership model that ensures shared goals and resources for co-design and co-implementation is used for maximum collective impact. The hub aims to showcase, optimize, and promote existing circular bioeconomy innovations while fostering the development of new, accessible innovations. In 2024, the co-owners of the hub agreed to formalize their collaboration under a Memorandum of Understanding.

description: Sixty-one fish seed multiplier hatcheries, including 18 Department of Fisheries facilities, the Bangladesh Fisheries Research Institute, one academic institution, and 41 private hatcheries, have adopted the faster-growing Generation 3 Rohu strain. Of these, 29 produced seed in 2024, while the remaining hatcheries await broodstock maturity for spawning in subsequent years. description: An agronomic assessment undertaken by the Initiative reveals that plant-based biopesticides derived from neem and chili extracts have proved effective in reducing pests’ incidence. In Kenya, neem-based biopesticides reduced fall armyworm incidence in maize by 5.2% and aphid incidence in beans by 22%. Similarly, chili-based biopesticides lowered brassica aphid incidence in cabbage by 5%. These trials, conducted by IITA, the Alliance of Bioversity & CIAT, CIFOR-ICRAF, DNRC, and CSHEP, revealed promising trends, though pest pressures were lower than typical conditions. Further testing under diverse climatic conditions and pest pressures is needed to confirm their efficacy in supporting integrated pest management (IPM) in diverse environments. Additionally, neem and chili biopesticides are being trialed in Zimbabwe and India, but results are still pending. Comprehensive data collection and analysis are crucial to validate the effectiveness of these biopesticides and ensure their optimal use in IPM across diverse agroecological systems.

description: An agronomic assessment undertaken by the Initiative reveals that animal manure plays a crucial role in agroecological systems, serving as organic fertilizer, soil conditioner, and input for bio-inputs. In Kenya (research conducted by IITA, Alliance Bioversity & CIAT, CIFOR-ICRAF, DNRC, and CSHEP), maize yields increased by 18%, and bean yields by 25%, when fertilized with 10 tons/ha of manure. However, applying 4 tons/ha of manure did not significantly increase spinach yields. Furthermore, cattle manure in Burkina Faso and horse manure in Senegal effectively boosted groundnut and millet production. For example, in Senegal, manure increased groundnut and cowpea yields as sole crops by 23% and 36%, respectively. These findings highlight the importance of manure as a strategic resource. However, achieving sustainable impacts requires a thorough understanding of its nutrient composition, availability, and optimal application rates for specific crops and contexts.
