description: The adoption and impacts of CGIAR-related maize varieties in 18 major maize-producing countries in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) during 1995–2015 was established. Of the 1345 maize varieties released during this timeframe, approximately 60% had known CGIAR parentage. About 34% (9.5 million ha) of the total maize area in 2015 was cultivated with CGIAR-related maize varieties released between 1995 and 2015. In the same year, an additional 13% of the maize area was cultivated with CGIAR-related maize varieties released before 1995. The aggregate annual economic benefit of using new CGIAR-related maize germplasm for yield increase in SSA was estimated at US$1.1–1.6 billion in 2015, which we attributed equally to co-investments by CGIAR funders, public-sector national research and extension programs, and private sector partners. The benefit-cost ratios for the CGIAR investment and CGIAR-attributable portion of economic benefits varied from 12:1–17:1, assuming a 5-year lag in the research investment to yield returns.
title: Impact of CGIAR maize germplasm in Sub-Saharan Africa: 1995-2015 Maize Varieties Adoption and Economic Benefits

description: Participatory rangeland management (PRM) is a CGIAR Livestock and Climate Initiative innovation that builds the capacities of pastoralists and other stakeholders to better secure, manage and govern their lands. The innovation has been piloted  and upscaled in Ethiopia, and is now being implemented in Kenya and Tanzania. It is different to other community-based natural resource management approaches in that emphasis is placed on communities leading the process, with technical partners supporting and facilitating. Independent impact evaluations have highlighted its positive benefits on good governance including greater gender equity, rangelands and livestock production systems. In 2023 IGAD (Intergovernmental Authority on Development) entered into an agreement with ILRI to produce a practitioners manual for implementing PRM across the IGAD region with the input and consultation of all member states through a regional workshop. The manual is being finalized and its dissemination will be followed by a training of trainers program.

description: The Gold Standard adopts the methodology for methane emission reduction by adjusted water management practice in rice cultivation developed by the Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) through the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI). The methodology is applicable to measures that reduce anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice-cropping soils. Such measures include changing the water regime during the cultivation period from continuously to intermittently flooded conditions and/or a shortened period of flooded conditions, using the alternate wetting and drying method, adopting aerobic rice cultivation methods, and switching from transplanted to direct-seeded rice (DSR). This methodology can be applied to large and small-scale or micro-scale projects.
title: Methodology for methane emission reduction by adjusted water management practice in rice cultivation adopted by Gold Standard in certifying climate mitigation and adaptation projects
input_text: The Gold Standard adopts the methodology for methane emission reduction by adjusted water management practice in rice cultivation developed by the Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) through the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI). The methodology is applicable to measures that reduce anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice-cropping soils. Such measures include changing the water regime during the cultivation period from continuously to intermittently flooded conditions and/or a shortened period of flooded conditions, using the alternate wetting and drying method, adopting aerobic rice cultivation methods, and switching from transplanted to direct-seeded rice (DSR). This methodology can be applied to large and small-scale or micro-scale projects. Methodology for methane emission reduction by adjusted water management practice in rice cultivation adopted by Gold Standard in certifying climate mitigation and adaptation projects

description: CIMMYT monitors the use of CIMMYT-derived maize hybrids and open pollinated varieties (OPVs) for commercialization through a systematic licensing strategy. Such calls are widely advertised. Both public and private sector institutions may apply and receive licenses to commercialize available hybrids. CIMMYT typically does not charge any licensing fees or royalties. Exclusivity is limited to national registration and commercialization activities only. CIMMYT and other partners who receive the materials from CIMMYT under the SMTA maintain the freedom to use the same hybrid for research, breeding and training activities, and CIMMYT may further allocate the same licensed hybrid to different organizations for registration and commercialization in other countries. License allocations are annually disclosed on CIMMYT's website and provides evidence on the use of CIMMYT-derived maize hybrids and OPVs. Between 2017 and 2022, 383 licenses were allocated to 239 public and private partners, evidence for wide access and use of CGIAR maize innovations.
title: Investments in CIMMYT collaborative maize breeding results in farmers gaining access to stress-tolerant, nutritious maize hybrids and varieties at large scale

description: The Scaling Scan is a self-assessment tool to help teams and partners explore what is required to scale an innovation in a particular context. It was developed and tested in 2017 by CIMMYT and the PPPLab and launched in 2018 . The theory underlying the Scaling Scan is based on an understanding of scaling as a process to contribute to sustainable systems change at scale as described in the paper by Woltering (et al., 2019). At the core of the Scaling Scan is a scalability assessment tool that integrates ten scaling “ingredients” (e.g., “Finance”, “Collaboration”, and “Awareness & Demand” etc), each reflecting particular sets of professional activities. Ubels and Jacobs (2016) found these ingredients to be critical for successful scaling. Nine out of ten scaling ingredients focus on the non-technological conditions that determine if the system around the innovation is “scale-friendly” (Woltering et al., 2019).

description: The forage hybrids developed by the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), in collaboration with the private forage seed sector, are important for increasing the productivity and quality feed for the cattle sector and thus contribute to improving food security, income, and livelihoods of cattle producing families. In addition to achieving this primary objective, the adoption of these technologies generates positive environmental externalities, such as a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. Plant breeding continues with the objectives of obtaining materials with higher nutritional quality, nitrogen-use-efficiency, and the ability to regenerate and avoid soil degradation. Colombia, Kenya, and Ethiopia are examples for countries, where cattle plays an important role for the rural population and the agricultural gross domestic product. Cattle production in these countries is mostly dependent on forage materials with low quality and scarcity of feeds happens frequently in prolonged dry seasons and under climate change. The adoption of Urochloa hybrids helps in this regard.

description: The Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) Morocco Use Case is propelling the advancement of Conservation Agriculture (CA) through focused initiatives. This involves a thorough update on CA research, concentrating on crop diversification and weed control, adapted to Morocco's diverse soil and climate. Emphasis is placed on data collection and analysis to uncover key factors influencing CA adoption, including an in-depth look at farmers' practices and barriers to CA adoption by 2030. A significant development is the pilot digital platform for CA monitoring, designed to track vital elements like soil health, crop rotation, and yield. This platform integrates CA suitability maps, identifying priority areas for effective scaling interventions. These concerted efforts aim to boost CA adoption, promoting sustainable agricultural productivity and environmental conservation in Morocco.

description: Six demand partners collaborated with the Excellence in Agronomy Initiative (EiA) to integrate various agronomic solutions (e.g., fertilizer recommendation tools for cassava, rice and maize) into different interfaces. Integrate this with other agricultural advisories like safe/optimum planting window, variety choice and good agricultural practice. ​All the Use Cases have implemented validation trials. description: Technical trainings of identified agroecological integrated pest management practices led to adoption by trained framers: Concoctions of neem and pepper, intercropping, crop rotation and crop diversity, Soil building and fertility mainly compost, animal manure, plant teas, liquid manure, among others. On water harvesting they were trained on sunken beds, terraces/swales, farm ponds, mini surface dams among others. DNRC observed that farmers have started embracing organic farming as they are now aware of the negative effects of synthetic chemicals. They started to conserve water with some embracing cover crops, tree planting, recycling of water and rain water harvesting due to ongoing trainings on agroecology. Farmers improved record keeping, train other farmers. DNRC started to receive schools visiting to showcase agroecological practices.

description: Accelerated Breeding has developed tools and approaches for taking stock of current breeding pipelines and mapping them to a portfolio of distinct, achievable target product profiles (TPP’s) - each a unique combination of productivity, adaptation, resilience, quality, processing and consumer traits. TPPs should be feasible, impactful, gender-relevant, and in-demand. By 30 November 2024, CGIAR breeding programs have aligned 157 Breeding Pipelines and 418 TPPs 1:1 to sub-regional market segments (418 out of 701 defined) using the Breeding Portal. Each TPP contains trait requirements and targeted scores. The traits are categorized through 14 value propositions that make breeding pipeline orientation toward Impact Areas transparent. Almost all (>95%) of CGIAR breeding programs have systematically oriented breeding pipelines towards farmers’ needs, drivers of adoption, and impact. 55% of all TPPs were informed by gender studies, gender specialists or gender-disaggregated on-farm feedback. Together, the TPPs target close to 400 million hectares grown by smallholders.

description: Fishbase and SeaLifeBase are online, publicly accessibly information systems on aquatic species. description: Continuing with efforts made by the Excellence in Breeding Platform, 128 in-depths assessments of NARES Breeding Programs have been done since 2019. Each partner assessment has been followed by NARES developing a customized improvement plan. So, far 93 NARES have completed them. These plans are the basis for developing individual and regional capacity development plans, increasing NARES engagement in regional collaborative breeding approaches, and modernizing regional breeding strategies, such as through centralized rapid cycle genomic selection and expanded on-farm testing at earlier stages. Network partners are using the improvement plans as a basis for internal and external funding applications, such as to Crops to End Hunger. The overall benefits are: 1. more targeted approaches to capacity development, 2. increased NARES capacity to participate in breeding networks and develop varieties, 3. stronger CGIAR-NARES collaborative efforts, and 4. a growing community of breeding teams accelerating genetic gains for major food crops.

description: In 2024, partner organizations in 42 countries registered a total of 287 crop varieties deriving from CGIAR breeding pipelines. They were improved in collaboration with over 600 partner organizations in Africa, Asia and Latin America. 58% varieties are climate-resilient. 26% are biofortified and directed to lower malnutrition among women and children, or are aimed at reducing cooking time with a gender differential impact. Variety releases are no guarantee for multiplication and use but they are an important milestone. Many countries require variety registration for commercialization. Variety registrations were from: Barley, Beans, Cassava, Chickpea, Faba bean, Groundnut, Lentil, Maize, Millet, Potato, Rice, Sorghum, Soybean, Sweetpotato, Wheat, and Yam. 150 varieties were registered in Africa (18 countries), 94 in Asia (11 countries), 39 in Latin America (11 countries), 4 in high-income countries. 78% were registered in low and lower-middle income economies inhabited by 93% of people with daily incomes below $2.15.

description: A user satisfaction survey among agricultural extension workers in Indonesia was conducted to assess their experiences with the Layanan Konsultasi Padi (LKP) platform after receiving training and disseminating its recommendations to rice farmers. The survey evaluated their knowledge of the platform, challenges encountered, and perceptions of its effectiveness. Results showed that 97% of respondents had a clear (84%, 103 of 122) or somewhat clear (13%, 16 of 122) understanding of how to use LKP to share nutrient management recommendations with farmers. Additionally, 85% found the platform relatively easy to use, and 89% considered it beneficial to farmers. LKP, developed by IRRI for the Indonesian context, is a digital agricultural decision-support tool that delivers tailored nutrient management recommendations based on site-specific nutrient management principles for rice fields.

description: The main dairy product consumed by the population of Bobo-Dioulasso is yogurt. The majority of dairy processors make yogurts based on imported milk powder and flavor the yogurts with artificial flavors. The Bobo-Dioulasso dairy processing units that are members of the Agroecology Living Landscape (and who are part of the Dairy Innovation Platform) that process locally produced fresh milk have started to diversify their yogurt production by flavoring them with natural extracts of non-timber forest products and local agricultural products (pineapple, sweet banana (poyo), coconut, date, ginger, horchata (chufa), kinkéliba, mango, mint, moringa, nere, monkey bread (théodo), orange-fleshed sweet potato, tamarind, zeguene (balanites)). And it works. There is an outlet for these yogurts that we can qualify as ''agroecological yogurts'' because they are made from real milk and flavored with local natural flavors.

description: The initial research strategy centered on a pioneering plant breeding method developed by an Australian team, known as BRIO. BRIO stands for accurate breeding values (using genomic and pedigree data), rapid breeding cycles, a selection index for multiple traits, and optimized mating designs via optimal contributions selection (OCS). Early in the project, theoretical results from BRIO applied to crops like canola showed promise. By year four, field trials by the Australian team confirmed superior breeding outcomes, particularly for grain yield and seed quality in commercial canola (Cowling et al., 2023) and improved traits in field peas with lower heritability (Castro-Urrea et al., 2023). This approach has now been adapted for common beans within the East and Central Africa Bean Research Network (ECABREN), under the Pan Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA). Breeding is based at the Alliance-CIAT in Uganda, with field trials for selection implemented across six partnering countries.
title: A robust breeding system (BRIO) for common bean established within the east and central Africa bean research network (ECABREN) component of the Pan Africa Bean

description: The one-million-hectare project, where the mechanized direct seeding technology is adopted by the government as key innovation for improved  productivity and rescued greenhouse gas emissions in rice, is implemented in 12 provinces and cities in the Mekong River Delta. Prior to widespread execution, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) established model sites in Can Tho City, Tra Vinh, Soc Trang, Kien Giang, and Dong Thap Provinces. The one-million-hectare program, with an emphasis on high quality, low-emission rice production and green growth in the Mekong Delta until 2030, is the first large-scale strategy in the worldwide rice sector. According to the Department of Crop Production (DCP), under MARD's guidance, seven pilot models have been carried out in five localities: Kien Giang, Soc Trang, Tra Vinh, Dong Thap, and Can Tho City, in conjunction with IRRI and private partners.

description: This outcome from the collaborative, non-pooled funding effort between Transforming Agrifood Systems in South Asia (TAFSSA) and the Cereal Systems Initiative for South Asia – Mechanization Extension Activity (CSISA–MEA), aligning with the initiative's theory of change. Agriculture-Based Light Engineering (ABLE) enterprises, in partnership with the Activity, reported total sales of USD 1,178,756 for this period. These results were facilitated by expanded market access through marketing events attended by lead firms, dealers, and Machinery Service Providers (MSPs), where ABLE enterprise partners, supported by the Activity, showcased their machines and parts. CSISA–MEA facilitated meetings between ABLE enterprises, dealers, MSPs, and Financial Services Institutions to strengthen partnerships and access to financial resources. Marketing events organized by the Activity significantly contributed to MSPs' purchases of machinery and spare parts. Notably, sales of combine harvesters accounted for 82% of the total funds generated. Women purchased 8% of the machines sold, underscoring an inclusive market impact.
title: Facilitation of scaling-out of business models with companies and machinery service providers that resulted in $1.2 million of new agricultural machinery sales in Bangladesh.

description: The Seed Equal (SE) initiative is transforming school meals in Malawi by integrating biofortified crops into the Home-Grown School Feeding Program (HGSFP). In collaboration with the Ministry of Education and supported by the European Union (EU) and the World Food Programme (WFP), SE has introduced nutrient-rich crops like high-iron beans, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes (OFSP), and orange maize flour in select schools across Southern Malawi. Training sessions for school feeding committees, lead farmers, and care group promoters have been conducted to enhance the production and utilization of these crops. Awareness meetings have also been held to promote the benefits of biofortified crops, aiming to improve nutrition and food security for school children.

description: The innovation is a bundle of three technologies for intensification of maize-small ruminants farming system in northern Ghana. The basal NPK fertilizer timing focuses on applying the fertilizer at planting stage of maize to reduce nutrient stress especially during the emergence-vegetative stage, enhance nutrient use efficiency and yield. Intercropping of cowpea at one week after planting of maize as a living mulch provides soil surface cover, increases soil moisture retention, adds nutrients through biological nitrogen fixation, suppresses weeds growth, and increases yield and food diversity. Harvesting of maize leaves below the cob leaf at silking stage (Leaf stripping) offers quality forage for livestock without compromising grain yield. The stripped maize leaf forage has a 40% higher crude protein content than the crude protein content of feed required for the body maintenance of livestock. Feeding strip maize leaf to small ruminants increases live body, slaughter, and carcass weights.

description: Maintaining inter-varietal crop diversity, created through evolutionary plant breeding (EPB), on farms is proven to improve farmers productivity, resilience to climate change and enhance dietary diversity. We have tested evolutionary populations created through Evolutionary Plant Breeding in Ethiopia, Bhutan, Iran, Jordan, Nepal and Uganda for four crops: Barley, beans, wheat and rice and identified superior performing populations under different farming systems. Integration of evolutionary plant breeding to Sustainable Intensification of Mixed farming System (SI-MFS) in target countries is important to sustain crop production sector of target farming systems. At least one composite or mixture population is developed for each country targeted by the SI-MFS initiative.

description: Good quality feed year-round is limiting livestock productivity on-farm and resource use in farms of small to medium size. Feed production can amount to 50 to 70% of livestock production costs. Forages are a means to overcome the feed gap, and resilient forages responding to different abiotic and biotic stresses, including low soil fertility, drought / excess water, pest diseases, are essential, increasing livestock productivity by up to 15%. To scale such technologies, suitable entry points i.e., market-oriented livestock production particularly dairy are required. Enablers are animal genetics and health technologies which capitalize on the improved feeding as well as capacity and dissemination channels such as cooperatives and functional seed supply systems. We are using a diversity of advanced forages which have a good availability of seed and/or planting material and demand pull through livestock production in Kenya; at the same time a pipeline for improved forages is being maintained.

description: Index-based drought risk financing and insurance (IBDRFI) instruments trigger payouts/financial response based on an ‘objective’ index approximating the impact/loss. The products have been designed to protect pastoralists in the face of drought. In Index-based livestock insurance (IBLI) products, Normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) time series are elaborated to obtain an area-aggregated index of relative seasonal forage availability. When the index falls below a pre-defined threshold, payouts are triggered and increase proportionally to the severity of estimated forage scarcity. This assumes that, when forage is scarce, grazing resources are depleted quickly, leading to deteriorating livestock conditions and increased livestock mortality. Pastoralists could use the payouts to make production decisions that reduce their herd losses during the drought including, purchasing animal fodder, water or veterinary services. IBDRFI initiatives have been implemented in Africa with different modalities, including retail microinsurance products, macrolevel insurance schemes for social livelihood protection, or social safety net programs.

description: Compressing local agro-industrial by products into nutrient dense livestock feed pellets is a worthwhile innovation to compete with expensive and imported feed pellets or concentrates. Use of such pellets also alleviates pressure on rangelands or grasslands.  This innovation consists of a small scale compressor 'pelletizer' and formulas to create qualitatively suﬃcient feed pellets with locally available inputs. In Tunisia, there are many agro-pastoralists that are dependent on expensive and imported livestock feed pellets to improve livestock quality and to supplement feed shortages. Risks of relative feed shortages are likely to increase due to climate change. Also there are many discarded by-products from local agro-food supply chains such as olive cakes, date kernels, and downgraded dates, which still contain nutrients. Feed pellet production with this small scale pelletizer producing 500 kg pellets / hour is also an interesting income generating activity for farmer organizations and creates employment.

description: Insufficient water availability in the mid-hills of Nepal, including many municipalities in Khotang and Surkhet districts, has negatively impacted agricultural productivity in the region. During the participatory innovation selection process for various components of the Mixed Farming System, local farmers identified micro-irrigation as a top-priority innovation to enhance agricultural output. description: The Environmental Flow Assessment Tools are a set of user-friendly (online and offline) software tools enabling quick estimation of coarsescale environmental flow requirements of rivers. The input data required are time series data of monthly “natural” river flows, either measured or estimated. The tools are meant to be used by water planners and managers in making initial planning-level estimates of environmental flows, which may then be followed by more comprehensive assessments using further data related to aquatic ecology, moving beyond river flow data. The tools are also useful for building capacity on environmental flow estimation, including for students and practitioners seeking to gain an initial understanding of the concept of environmental flows. The IPSR assessment conducted in Pakistan is a first step towards understanding the enabling environment for scaling this innovation and identifying complementary innovations required for scaling.

description: Working toward this objective, experts in social norms measurement from FHI360, an international development organization based in Washington, DC worked with IFPRI and IITA to co-develop a survey instrument to measure inequitable social and gender norms within cassava, fish, and chicken Agri-Food-Systems (AFS). The index can be used to inform the design of gender-transformative approaches to address harmful social and gender norms in AFS.

description: In Colombia, the sector that contributes the most to national emissions is Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU), where the loss of natural forests for conversion to other land uses has a significant impact. Monitoring non-deforestation associated with agricultural and livestock supply chains at the farm level is a challenge. Therefore, one of the main challenges faced by the public-private initiative of the Zero Deforestation Agreements is to develop agile, cost-effective, and transparent tools and protocols to monitor compliance with non-deforestation commitments in these supply chains. The document provides a guide for information collection and the processes of MRV (Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification) of non-deforestation resulting from agricultural activities, thus contributing activity data to national inventories.

description: Nomadic livestock systems have evolved over millennia as a response to seasonal rainfall patterns. In Tunisia, where approximately one-third of the land is semi-arid, arid, or desert, degradation poses a significant challenge. The Gdel resting technique, a low-cost intervention, has been part of the national strategy for rangeland improvement Since 1990, this practice is implemented by developing agencies for rangeland improvement. The pastoralists whose animals would normally graze in these areas are supported through the provision of feed supplements for 3 consecutive years. However, the implementation had its shortfalls. However, in 2018, unexpectedly high rainfall led to abundant vegetation growth, but the rigid implementation of the resting technique hindered pastoralists from capitalizing on the surplus biomass. In response, ICARDA developed flexible grazing criteria and trained partners to adapt to climate variability. This innovative approach allows pastoralists to optimize resource utilization during favorable years and addressing the shortcomings of previous implementations.

description: The Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB) is an approach provides climate advisory services to smallholder farmers in Vietnam using seasonal, monthly, and 10-day weather forecasts. description: The Africa RISING Ethiopian Highlands project, a predecessor to the Mixed Farming System Initiative validated and promoted various forage species. description: The 'GANSO Endorsement' is a voluntary evaluation tool for livestock producers. We support them in developing a farm-level adapted scaling approach complementary to existing institutions, involving pioneers themselves as the main actors in the scaling process. Together with the pioneers we study their practices, and then progressively include more farmers, farmer groups, cooperatives in a knowledge exchange through participatory field days where pioneers share and discuss the findings of this data collection on their practices. Gradually, we develop a Farmer2Farmer knowledge network that connects pioneers and their learning groups with research, extension, development organisations, and private sector actors.
title: Innovation Package and Scaling Readiness assessment for tools for pioneer farmer-led scaling and knowledge network development by pioneer farmers, researchers, extension, private and development actors for outscaling on-farm adaptation to climate change. in Ethiopia

description: The Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) initiative in Ethiopia tackles key challenges in agriculture, including low productivity and inefficient fertilizer use in staple crops like maize, wheat, teff, and sorghum. To address these issues, EiA supported the development of the Harmonized Digital Fertilizer and Agronomic Solutions (HaFAS) framework—co-created by national institutions (MoA, EIAR, RARIs) and CGIAR centers (ICRISAT, CIAT). HaFAS integrates decades of agronomic data, soil databases, and remote sensing into a unified digital advisory system. Its core tool, the Localized Agronomy and Fertilizer Advisory (LAFA), was validated across 1,570 fields in 2024 and provides site-specific, climate-resilient recommendations through chatbots, SMS, mobile apps, and other channels. Aligned with Ethiopia’s Digital Agriculture Roadmap 2032, LAFA improves fertilizer efficiency, supports sustainable intensification, and enhances the return on the government’s $1.2 billion annual fertilizer investment—offering a scalable, evidence-based approach to transform Ethiopia’s agricultural productivity and resilience.

description:
The Smart Nkunganire System (SNS) was created in response to the Rwandan Ministry of Agriculture's (MINAGRI) request for enhanced digital extension services and precise, site-specific fertilizer recommendations for essential crops. The project aims to develop a digital advisory tool integrated within the existing SNS platform, managed by BKTechouse. This tool is designed to provide customized fertilizer recommendations for six priority crops in Rwanda: cassava, maize, wheat, potato, rice, and beans, making these recommendations accessible to both extension agents and farmers through the SNS platform._x000D_
_x000D_
This initiative is further supported by making these tools and methodologies available to the Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resources Development Board (RAB), aiming to enhance the innovation's development. This strategic approach ensures that the digital advisory tool effectively meets the specific needs of Rwanda's agriculture sector, providing tailored support to improve productivity and sustainability.

description: Participatory Rangeland Management (PRM) is a defined step-by-step process for improving local level rangeland management by local pastoralist communities. It follows three stages of investigation (including participatory mapping), negotiation and implementation. It supports establishment and/or strengthening of rangelands management institutions, and supports the production of a rangeland management plan and an agreement with local government to improve access of communities to natural resources and land. M&E and capacity building are also important steps.

description: Farmer groups are core for improved farmers' access to input and output markets, as well as being a forum for capacity development and co-create of solutions to issues pertaining to pig and cattle keeping. description: PigSMART platform delivers digital extension messages to pig farmers. It covers an integrated content that is delivered to pig farmers based on the stage of growth of the pigs. The messages include best practices in feeding, herd health management, breeding and genetics, manure management and heat stress management. The process of integrating and adapting the content followed key steps: (i) curation of research outputs on feeds, health, genetics, and heat stress, (ii) drawing messages from the research outputs, (iii) validating messages from the researchers and government extension  to ensure integrity of content, (iv) integrating messages premised on the different stages of pig growth, and (v) developing audio skits from integrated content in Luganda. A brochure on the integrated content was developed and disseminated to pig farmers in addition to the audio skits. The messages can be used by extension agents to train farmers on best practices in pig production.

description: Breeding programs that are community-based cover a range of situations. Typically, they target low input systems with farmers within a limited geographical area who have a common interest to work together for the improvement of the genetic resources of their animals. Community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) focus on indigenous stock and consider farmers’ needs, views, decisions and active participation, from inception through to implementation. Most importantly, they provide a participatory and bottom-up approach. CBBP combines farmer training to improve selection methods, consisting of pooling community flocks to create a larger gene pool from which breeding animals can be selected, scientific support to provide farmers with information on different breeding options and data collection to monitor how well individual animals perform. The entire community flock is treated as one. Livestock keepers who choose to participate in the program are organized into sheep/goat breeding associations, many of which later evolve into formal cooperatives.

description: Point of Cow is a disposable chip manufactured by Fluimedix (Denmark).  It is a compact and user-friendly diagnostic tool that serves as a crucial component in antibiotic treatment decision making. The chip is engineered to detect both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria within 4-24hrs,  enabling quick decision-making on whether to use antibiotic treatment for mastitis. Point of Cow is primarily designed for dairy farmers, but can also be used by milk processors and quality control professionals in the dairy industry. It is a valuable tool for anyone involved in milk production and processing.

description: The WELI facilitates assessments of the impact of livestock interventions on the empowerment of women involved in the sector. By getting better at understanding what interventions work best at providing empowering opportunities, we can refine these interventions and in the long term, provide better empowering opportunities for women involved in livestock. Providing women farmers with opportunities for empowerment through livestock is important to both enhance household livelihoods and nutrition while also promoting progress on gender equity. In 2015, the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), in collaboration with Emory University developed the WELI tool based on the Women’s Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI) developed earlier by IFPRI. The WELI measures women’s empowerment in livestock and crop agriculture and focuses specifically on key areas of livestock production, such as animal health, breeding and feeding; and on use of livestock products, such as animal-source-food processing and marketing.

description: A package combining gender accommodative and transformative approaches to deliver improved chickens, animal services and markets to women farmers by women veterinarians. Gender accommodative approaches were adopted to enhance the business and chicken management skills of the women vets. Gender transformative approaches (in this case social media) were adopted to address gender norms that make women’s involvement in chicken business socially inappropriate. Restrictive gender norms are considered the root cause of gender-based disadvantage; unlike gender accommodative approaches, gender transformative approaches aim to change such restrictive norms for lasting social change.

description: The One Health Unit (OHU) serves as a collaboration and coordination platform for frontline service providers and community-based actors to deliver integrated services to improve the health of humans, animals and the environment. In mobile OHUs, frontline service providers move along pastoralist/livestock routes, according to a monthly schedule, changing sites every day and responding to the needs of the population in a certain site/location. In static OHUs, frontline service providers work side by side in a common facility (e.g., human/animal health post, water point or other village gathering site). The OHU is generally staffed by government employees from different sectors who are released from their regular duties to deliver integrated services through the OHU. The services are targeted towards pastoralist and agropastoralist communities, their livestock, and the rangelands which they access, with a particular focus on vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities.

description: Conservation Agriculture (CA) is based on three key principles: minimum soil disturbance, provision of permanent soil cover and the use of rotations or associations amongst other good agriculture practices. These CA principles are applicable to a wide range of crop production systems from low-yielding, rain-fed conditions to high-yielding, irrigated conditions. However, the techniques used may vary from place to place depending on farm power, system management conditions and farmer circumstances. CA aims at rebuilding the soil, optimizing crop production inputs especially labour, and increasing profits. The social and economic benefits gained from combining production and protecting the environment under CA, including reduced input and labour costs, are greater than those from production alone. With CA, farming communities become providers of more healthy living environments for the wider community through reduced use of fossil fuels and through conservation of environmental integrity and services.

description: This innovation involves incorporation of coarsely-ground Mucuna pruriens grain as a unique, cost-effective ingredient and energy-protein dense substitute in maintenance or fattening rations of ruminant livestock, where standard commercial supplements would usually contain a combination of cereal grains (e.g. maize) and legume oil cakes (e.g Soyabean, cotton seed etc), which are themselves generally expensive.  These expensive ingredients make the commercial concentrates out of reach for most farmers.  In contrast, Mucuna is cheaper and provides both energy and protein in one grain.  Once ground, the Mucuna meal will be constituted together with home-made tropical forage legumes (e.g. Lablab purpureus) hay to make a complete diet which smallholder farmers can brand and trade among themselves. Incorporation of legume hay reduces the amount of poor quality grass hay and cereal crop residues that will be included as basal forage in the complete diet and will simultaneously improve the digestibility of the poor quality residues, leading to improved animal growth.

description: Double-row strip cropping: This system reduces the plant spacing of maize rows to open up space for legumes to grow. Maize is usually intercropped with a legume (i.e., groundnuts/soya beans/cowpeas/beans). Maize is planted into rip-lines opened in double rows (50cm inter-row x 25cm in-row) and a gap of 130cm is left in-between the maize double rows where legumes will be planted [groundnut (35cm inter-row x 30cm in-row); soya beans (35cm inter-row x 5cm in-row)]Four-row strip cropping: Similar to double row strip cropping above, four rows of maize alternate with four rows of a legume. However, the inter-row spacing of maize is reduced from the usual 90 cm to 45 cm. This narrowing and reduction in size increases growing space for four rows of legumes. Maize is planted into lines spaced at 45 cm inter-row with 4 row strips of maize alternating with another 4 rows strip of soya beans/groundnuts also spaced at 45 cm between rows.

description: In Nigeria, processing cassava for food and industry yields around 15 million tons of wet peels annually. These peels are usually dumped near processing centres to rot or dry enough to be burned. Rotting heaps release methane into the air and a stinking effluent that pollutes nearby streams and underground water, while burning produces clouds of acrid smoke. However, when properly dried, peels can be an ingredient in animal feed. Previous attempts over two decades to use peels in animal feed failed to yield profitable options for drying wet peels at commercial scale, but recent research suggests that cassava peels can be processed into high-quality cassava peel (HQCP) products to be used as nutritious, low-cost animal feed ingredients by livestock feed suppliers and their customers (livestock-keepers)

description: A data-to-analytics infrastructure roadmap was developed for EiA in 2022. A critical part of this infrastructure is a global data pool or database that allows search within standardized datasets (i.e., beyond traditional metadata search) to return aggregated datasets that can directly be used for analyses. A proof-of-concept data pool was developed in Q4 of 2022, built on state-of-the-art graph database technology, with an alpha version released in 2023. Users can search the database for gender-disaggregated data, to assess gender-based differences in crop yields or fertilizer application rates. The aggregated data returned from such searches is pre-formatted for easier use in analytical tools (aligned with R scripts as for the Carob model) and for commonly-used AgMIP crop simulation models (as a first step toward data-to-model capability).

description: CIP Mozambique tested 11 pre-released clones under on-farm for multi-stakeholder validation across five provinces (Niassa, Nampula, Zambezia, Manica and Inhambane) ensuring representation of diverse environments and farmer conditions. description: The International Potato Center together with national agriculture research programs (Malawi, Zambia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Rwanda and Uganda) finalized target product profiles with thresholds of priority traits determined. Capabilities of national research programs are different, and some depend on products developed in other countries for agronomic testing and variety release.

description: Access to adapted and market-preferred vegetable varieties is critical to increase production and supply. Before the FRESH interventions in Benin started, only 10 locally released tomato, pepper, onion, and African eggplant were registered in the national seed catalog. Many of them did not match the needs of farmers and consumers and were susceptible to diseases. For example, available tomato varieties were susceptible to bacterial wilt, which can cause 100% yield loss and has led farmers in the Valley of Ouémé, a major vegetable production area, to abandon tomato production totally. Overall the  limited variety choice for farmers was a great obstacle for vegetable production. The FRESH Initiative has introduced WorldVeg vegetable breeding lines to Benin that match major market segments and target product profiles.

description: Through collaborative research and action, ICARDA and the Tunisian government have co-pioneered opportunistic grazing as an innovative approach to sustainable rangeland management and included in the co-published IUCN-ICARDA Sustainable Rangeland Management toolkit, guided by scientific principles and enriched by local knowledge. Opportunistic grazing involves allowing livestock to graze on available forage during favorable conditions, ensuring optimal resource utilization. By adopting this approach, rangeland managers can maximize forage use, enhance ecosystem health, and achieve livestock production goals. This strategy has proven particularly effective in restoring rangelands and strengthening ecosystem resilience in Tunisia’s semi-arid regions. Recognizing its transformative potential, the Tunisian government has integrated opportunistic grazing into its rangeland management policies, updating regulations to formalize this sustainable practice. To date, this innovation has positively impacted 180,000 hectares, directly benefiting 6,212 individuals and contributing to long-term rangeland restoration and sustainability.

description: Quantification of crop stresses for targeted intervention, drone data was collected weekly to capture high-resolution imagery for monitoring crop biotic stresses, including diseases and pest infestations. This imagery helped map spatial disease patterns and assess the progression of stresses across different crops. Various analytical approaches were tested to refine detection techniques and improve early warning systems. Additionally, drone-based observations were compared with satellite imagery to evaluate differences in spatial and temporal resolution, ensuring a comprehensive assessment of crop health. The integration of these data sources enhanced the accuracy of stress detection, enabling timely interventions. The findings contribute to developing advanced biotic stress monitoring frameworks, supporting precision agriculture through early stress diagnosis and targeted management strategies. This research will enable researchers to integrate Earth observation technologies into crop health monitoring, improving resource management and resilience in agricultural systems, particularly in semi-arid regions where timely stress detection is crucial for sustainable farming.

description: Despite breakthroughs in genetic innovation, there is limited rigorous causal empirical evidence of the impacts of new varieties on smallholders’ livelihoods to justify investments in genetic innovation. Most estimates of the returns on investments in breeding are either modeling-based or stem from correlational rather than causal evidence. To fill this gap, Genetic Innovation started a new approach to impact assessment: designing and implementing a series of coordinated impact evaluations across CGIAR centers. The focus on impacts, coordination across centers, and the rigorous nature of these evaluations offers a more comprehensive approach to understanding how new varieties affect smallholders. Four proposals for randomized evaluations with implementation in India, Kenya and Malawi (HarvestPlus) were selected through a competitive proposal and the portfolio of coordinated impact assessments was launched through a workshop on October 24-25 in Nairobi. The workshop was the first step in aligning methodologies to ensure consistency across these four studies.
title: Four randomized impact evaluations of genetic innovations and seed system interventions from multiple CGIAR centers were selected and launched during a workshop in Nairobi

description: The innovations in (name the work package) have brought about significant benefits for many workers across various case-study settings. In Bangladesh, 210 recipients, half of whom are women, received financed livestock, directly improving their livelihoods. In Nigeria, 286 individuals, including 15% women, benefited from loans that provided much-needed financial support. Meanwhile, in Uganda, the EzyAgric digital services platform trained 513 individuals and engaged 191 agents, enhancing their skills and opportunities. Indirectly, the scale-up activities informed by these case studies have extended WeGro financing to an additional 1,768 recipients. This brings the total number of beneficiaries to 2,968, which is close to the EOIO target of 3,000. When considering the scale-up activities in Uganda and the indirect benefits to household members, the impact is even more substantial. The average household size is 4.3 in Bangladesh, 10.9 in Nigeria, and 6.5 in Uganda, further amplifying the reach of these initiatives. The gender-sensitive nature of the offers in the Bangladesh study ensures that both gender and youth targets are met, highlighting the inclusive approach of these efforts. Overall, the WP3 innovations have not only enriched the lives of the direct beneficiaries but also created a ripple effect, benefiting many more through extended family and community networks.

description: The introduction of machinery has increased men’s participation in post-harvesting activities like threshing, which were traditionally labeled as women's roles. Initiative research on the experiences and agency of diverse farmers provided insights into the potential for mechanization to mitigate gaps in men’s resources and opportunities as well as their tendency to experience a decline in agency as they aged, while also revealing to community participants the shared benefits of a mechanized and collaborative approach to post-harvest activities. Mechanization has also fostered collaborations between NGOs and farmers with 2 operators in Mbire supplying hay bales for other projects in the district. The operators are receiving coupons from the Environmental Management Agency (EMA) to collect grass as a way of reducing veld fires and promoting environmental conservation.

description:
In response to the growing demand for WEAI surveys, the CGIAR GENDER Impact Platform's Methods Module developed a distance learning course on pro-WEAI. This online course teaches specific skills related to using pro-WEAI to meet the needs of various users: quantitative analysts, monitoring & evaluation specialists, donors, and field supervisors. Participants will receive digital certification upon successful completion of the course. The Pro-WEAI Foundations Module is available in English, French, and Arabic. This module introduces researchers and practitioners to the pro-WEAI tool, covering its background and practical application within project contexts. This module provides conceptual frameworks, resources, and approaches to integrating the index tools into projects, based on real-world experiences from the team that developed it. Completion of the Foundations Module is a prerequisite for all subsequent modules. The subsequent modules build on the Foundations Module and include:_x000D_
Survey Fieldwork: Learn how to administer pro-WEAI surveys, from planning enumerator training to pilot testing and data collection. This module covers survey questions, response options, and fieldwork strategies._x000D_
Qualitative Analysis: Explore the qualitative methods used in pro-WEAI, including the rationale behind including qualitative methods, detailed protocols for different types of respondents, best practices for planning qualitative studies, and guidance on conducting analysis and disseminating results from qualitative pro-WEAI protocols._x000D_
Calculating the Index: Learn how to calculate pro-WEAI indicators and the pro-WEAI score. This module covers how to use the Stata do- and ado-files, read output tables and figures, and apply the results to your projects._x000D_
Interpreting and Presenting Pro-WEAI Results: Learn how to interpret both the qualitative and quantitative findings from pro-WEAI surveys. This module focuses on deriving insights for future programming and project management, building on the previous modules.

description: OEP (Office des Elevages et des Pâturages) has integrated biofertilization technology into its activities, making Rhizobium inoculation for forage legumes a key part of its strategy. This shift has been supported by participatory trials with farmers, leading to a voluntary increase in the adoption of sulla. OEP is now seeking additional funding from GIZ and other donors to establish a rhizobium unit to scale up specific forage crops in Tunisia. The initiative initiated a rhizobia experiment in Rhahla in 2022 to address soil fertility and climate change. This, alongside ongoing demonstrations with PROSOL-ICARDA, has influenced OEP's decision-makers, prompting them to request GIZ’s support for the investment. The experiment was supported by GIZ, with changes driven by partnerships with ICARDA under various initiatives, including IFAD-CLCA and GIZ-ICARDA-ProSol. The creation of a rhizobium inoculation unit is essential for OEP's goal to diversify local forage resources.

description: International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and the Africa Group of Negotiators Expert Support (AGNES) identified that countries were not aligning their capacity for implementation with their response to the UNFCCC. In response, IWMI and AGNES have developed an NDC Capacity Scorecard to provide an objective measure for countries to ascertain whether they have the capability to meet their NDC targets and identify potential areas for capacity building in government and national institutions. It is important for countries to have this understanding of their capability to deliver, given that they  will be held to account for the targets that are set. The consequence of only focusing on ever increasing targets for emissions reduction is that most countries in the Global South don’t have the capacity to achieve the targets, which sets them up for failure. A critical consideration is how to achieve a “whole of government” approach that links the business and private sector to develop a collaborative, sustainable approach. In a session held at the recent COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, this question was explored with inputs from South Africa, Kenya, Uganda and the National Business Initiative of South Africa.

description: This toolkit is composed by guidelines, a manual, and example Power Point slides to update exogenous yield growth. The toolkit is expected to be used during the preparation and implementation of the expert consultations for review and updating of exogenous yield growth parameters to 2050 in the International Model for Policy Analysis of Agricultural Commodities and Trade (IMPACT) of the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI). These exogenous yield growth parameters, commonly referred to as “Intrinsic Productivity growth Rates” (IPRs), represent a component of agricultural productivity that cannot be attributed to price effects, climate change and water shocks — elements which are explicitly captured by IMPACT. Yield growth from IPRs can represent, for example, new technologies, better management, improved input use efficiency, etc. Estimating IPRs to 2050 can be better understood as an exercise to derive future yield growth parameters from an informed extrapolation of observed past trends.

description: This study brings together an expanded set of evidence on the diffusion and productivity impact of CGIAR crop research through 2020, and breaks out these impacts by crop, region, and over time. It was developed by two CGIAR-external authors. It is one of the most comprehensive studies on the impact of CGIAR crop innovations. The study found that by 2016–2020, CGIAR-related crop technologies had been adopted on at least 221 million hectares across Asia, Africa and Latin America, generating economic welfare gains of $47 billion annually. In addition to raising farm income, productivity gains in staple crops have lowered food prices, thereby benefitting the whole population. This is a key reason why agricultural productivity growth, and food crop productivity growth in particular, has had greater impacts on poverty reduction in low-income countries than comparable productivity growth in other sectors.

description: This use case focuses on delivering tailored climate information to farmers in two districts of Odisha. The project aims to provide location-specific climate advisories, including weather forecasts and farming recommendations, to help farmers make informed decisions about their agricultural activities. The survey found that the ISAT Climate Information Services is the most commonly used source of weather information among farmers in Odisha (39%). By providing context-specific information, the project supports farmers in optimizing their farming practices, managing climate risks, and improving overall productivity. The study also investigates how farmers use this information in their decision-making processes, highlighting the impact of climate advisories on their choices regarding crop selection, sowing time, and other critical farming operations. Ultimately, this work seeks to understand how digital climate services can empower farmers and enhance the resilience of their farming systems.

description: The Zambia Drought Management System incorporates multisource information, namely access to real-time weather updates and open-access satellite data, that provides farmers, extension workers, agriculture and water resources authorities with all the information needed to forecast, monitor and manage drought. Specifically, it provides seasonal, sub-seasonal and seven-day weather forecasts to indicate when drought is present. The system incorporates national- to regional-level datasets drawn from multiple satellites, observed data and other sources. Zambia launched ZADMS on February 28, 2023 and it provides Zambia’s Ministry of Agriculture (MOA) all the information needed to effectively manage drought. Currently, it is used for drought risk mitigation and enabling timely action by national, state, and district level government authorities such as the Ministry of Agriculture and development organizations. This has helped to cushion smallholders, many of them poor, from the worst effects of a prolonged drought situation

The system incorporates national- to regional-level datasets drawn from multiple satellites, observed data and other sources. Zambia launched ZADMS on February 28, 2023 and it provides Zambia’s Ministry of Agriculture (MOA) all the information needed to effectively manage drought. Currently, it is used for drought risk mitigation and enabling timely action by national, state, and district level government authorities such as the Ministry of Agriculture and development organizations. This has helped to cushion smallholders, many of them poor, from the worst effects of a prolonged drought situation Zambia Drought Management System (ZADMS) Platform launched and used by Zambia Ministry of Agriculture to mitigate drought risks

description: The Women's Empowerment in Migration Index (WEMI) measures the multiple dimensions of agency, resources and achievements of female migrants. It builds on CGIAR's large body of work in developing women's empowerment metrics. The WEMI tries to unpack empowerment along the entire migration pathway looking at women's decision making about migration and work, control over assets and income, attitude towards employer violence, access to social networks, access to training and various aspects of self-efficacy and mental health as a migrant.
title: The Women's Empowerment in Migration Index (WEMI) helps governments, development partners and practitioners understand sources of and dynamics of disempowerment of women migrants.

description: The Zambia Ministry of Green Economy and Environment along with the CGIAR Initiative on Climate Resilience launched the Climate Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard in Lusaka in October 2023. The dashboard seeks to address the lack of timely, context-specific, actionable information for researchers, policy makers and planners to support evidence-based policy formulation for climate action. The Ministry of Green Economy and Environment Permanent Secretary, Dr. Douty Chibamba said "the establishment of this platform is timely. It will complement the national climate change communication and advocacy strategy for [the] ministry". He added that the dashboard is crucial given that climate change requires huge quantities of data to support decision making for adaptation planning at local, national, and transnational scales.

description: The Digital AgroClimate Advisory platform has developed a methodology to tailor some of its components to specific countries. This methodology was initially implemented in Ghana, and this involves: (1) service creation, (2) integration of data and contextualization and (3) service delivery, which involves customization of the systems to different conditions such as country or agro-ecological contexts. Service creation involves two steps: (1) collecting data on three major parameters (weather and climate data, soil data and crop characteristics) followed by (2) analysis of data that includes the analytics and climate/weather models, etc. Service delivery involves two steps: (1) bundling weather and climate information together with the crop information (such as crop water requirements, days to maturity, etc.) and crop fertilizer recommendations, and (2) delivering through DACA mobile app.

description: The Mekong River Delta (MRD). one of Southeast Asia's largest and most productive deltas, contributes 50% of Vietnam's total rice production.Recently, market demands have increased significantly, and importing countries have imposed stricter regulations, necessitating the enhancement of rice quality and assurance of food safety. description: In 2023, the Prime Minister approved Viet Nam's new National Action Plan for Transparent, Responsible, and Sustainable Food Systems Transformation (2022–2030), also known as FST-NAP. A guidance document developed in 2022 by the Institute of Policy and Strategy for Agriculture and Rural Development (IPSARD) and the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) with support from Sustainable Healthy Diets, has become a resource for people working in different levels of government to implement the new FST-NAP. For example, key terminologies appeared in the national implementation workshop in November and at follow-up workshops at the provincial level. In addition, CGIAR researchers involved in this Initiative and Asian Mega-Deltas are developing a similar type of guidance document to support local implementation of Viet Nam's National Action Program on "Zero Hunger," which is led by the Department of Cooperatives and Rural Development (DCRD) under MARD.

description: A Food System Country Profile is a web-based product that synthesizes critical information necessary for decisionmakers to obtain a holistic but synthetic overview of the components that are recognized to be critical for the sustainability of countries’ food systems. They are constructed and designed to identify hotspots of unsustainability in food systems and prioritize interventions at multiple scales to address these through targeted actions and investments.  In 2023, the Profile for Ethiopia was cited in a food systems training manual being developed by the government. The Government of Honduras mentioned the Profiles in their voluntary progress review for the United Nations Food Systems +2 Stocktaking Moment and the Ministry of Agriculture has outlined plans to replicate the methodology in 22 municipalities, starting in 2024. (Note: Honduras is a phase 2 country for Sustainable Healthy Diets).
title: Food System Country Profiles, concise snapshots decisionmakers in Ethiopia and Honduras have used to steer food systems transformation processes

description: A 36-minute video drama was produced for households in Addis Ababa to promote healthy eating habits. Through the dramatization featuring local actors, the video gives general advice on healthy eating with more explanation on how eating fruits and vegetables can lead to better health and nutrition. Two versions of the video were tested in the field. One mirrored the messages Ethiopia's health extension workers currently deliver and the other went into more explanation about how eating fruits and vegetables can lead to better health and nutrition. Four months after viewing either version, the average household consumption of fruits and vegetables increased by about 9 percent in both treatment groups relative to the control group, in terms of both kilocalories and consumption expenditure.
title: Video drama developed and tested to encourage urban consumers in Ethiopia to eat more fruits and vegetables

description: A demand-led seed system (DLSS) is an approach that places traders at the center of breeding and seed distribution, ensuring a steady supply of prioritized seeds into the system. Pan-Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA): A network of bean researchers and development partners that has successfully implemented the DLSS approach since the early 2000s in several countries. Notable findings show that the DLSS approach has led to a significant increase in the share (over 48%) of improved bean varieties in traders’ portfolios (averaging between 7 and 12 years old), a faster adoption process, a growing commercialization of new varieties (account for between 45% and 92.5%) of certified seed production, and a doubling of seed businesses. The DLSS model is also being applied to cowpeas in Ghana and Nigeria, demonstrating its potential as an effective approach for introducing and improving varieties and targeting niche markets.
title: Making Legume Seed Systems Efficient Through Demand-Led Approaches in Sub-Saharan Africa.

description: Cowpea is a major staple food for household nutrition and animal feed in sub-Saharan Africa. It is a food security crop and a cheap protein source for over 72% of households in West Africa. However, the cowpea seed business is poorly functioning resulting in a weak seed system characterized by a lack of product awareness, unpredictable seed demand, inefficient market and pricing systems. IITA is testing the off-taker/trader centered (demand-driven seed system) approach developed by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT to enhance the sector. So far, prioritizing and adopting the three improved varieties (SAMPEA 11, FUAMPEA 3 and FUAMPEA 4) increased certified/quality declared seeds production from 156.7 tons during the first year (2022) to 822.2 tons in the second year (2023), a fivefold increase. Within two years of the release of FUAMPEA 3 and 4 have become the fastest-demanded varieties in the cowpea seed value chain.
title: Adapting a Demand-led Seed System to Cowpea to Facilitate Variety Turnover: A Case Study in Nigeria

description: This innovation is part of this Initiative's strategy to build in-country partner capacity to use evidence and advocate for a focus on sustainable healthy diets in food systems transformation (FST) policy processes and improve food systems governance. The e-course has four modules on the food systems approach, food systems analysis, the process of FST, and FST governance, plus a Network Café to facilitate interaction and networking. The e-course was designed by the Wageningen Centre for Development Innovation and has been offered to more than 1450 participants to date. Under Sustainable Healthy Diets, the e-course has been offered to two cohorts of food systems actors (nearly 200 combined) in the Initiative's target countries. In response to partner demand in Viet Nam and Ethiopia, this Initiative and national partners are co-developing a training of trainers program, inspired by the e-course.
title: Food systems governance e-course expanded to support more actors working on food systems transformation in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and Viet Nam

description: The country coordination units (CCUs) in the Sustainable Healthy Diets target countries are a central part of the Initiative's strategy to strengthen the connections between CGIAR researchers and national partners in food systems policy processes. In 2023, two Viet Nam CCU meetings were held to share updates on the Initiative's research activities and to consult with the three government partners, also known as Strategic Partners, on progress and opportunities relative to food systems transformation in Viet Nam. The CCU, coordinated by the Sustainable Healthy Diets Country Coordinator, was instrumental in several other results reported in this year's annual report, including participation in the development of the government's new food systems partnership and several other aspects of implementation of the Food Systems Transformation National Action Plan (FST-NAP), the launch of a new training of trainers program on food systems, and preparation for the 2023 United Nations Food Systems +2 Stocktaking Moment.

description: The Foresight Community of Practice (CoP) aims to bring together foresight researchers and practitioners interested in transforming food, land, and water systems, with a focus on low and lower-middle-income countries. This is our community. The practices we are interested in discussing include models and tools, data and metrics, and practical foresight analysis for enhanced priority setting, policy, and investment decision-making. Note that these practices range from back-end model development and data analytics to generate actionable metrics, to the use of this knowledge for decision-making support. The Foresight CoP has a discussion forum for its members to exchange information and knowledge and to engage in meaningful discussions on a wide variety of foresight-related topics.

description: Here we report the adoption of Urochloa hybrid, an improved forage grass, by farmers within the SAPLING focal countries of Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Vietnam, for the years 2022 / 2023.  The numbers of adopters is estimated based on the numbers of hectares sown, farm size, and household size. We use the higher value of 2022 or 2023 to avoid double counting of households that adopted in both years.  The total number of people within adopting households is estimated as  70,015. This comprises: 43,434 for Uganda (2023 figure); 22,031 for Kenya (2022); 2,621 for Vietnam (2022); and 1,929 for Ethiopia (2022).  Note that support to Urochloa hybrid distribution has been provided by SAPLING over these years.
title: Adoption of the Urochloa hybrid improved forage grass by farmers within Ethiopia, Kenya,  Uganda and Vietnam

description: Piloting activities for the fertilizer recommendation tool within Rwanda’s Smart Nkunganire System (SNS) were conducted, reaching diverse participants across various regions. The innovation engaged extension agents and smallholder farmers, incorporating age and sex-disaggregated data. Multiple scaling channels (digital platforms, SMS, and community demonstrations) and formats were used, providing valuable insights to refine the tool for site-specific recommendations tailored to six priority crops: cassava, maize, wheat, potato, rice, and beans. The tool addresses Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources (MINAGRI) call for enhanced digital extension services, supporting productivity and sustainability in Rwanda's agriculture sector.

description: Until recently, water was notably absent from the national One Health planning and committees, where human, animal, and environmental health converge to address complex health challenges. However, Ethiopia’s Water Champions have intervened to ensure that water assumes its rightful central position within the One Health framework. Water management experts from relevant institutions are now identified and nominated to serve on national One Health committees. These experts participate in comprehensive training programs and are equipped with the necessary knowledge to inform committee deliberations on the role of water in pathogen transmission and on water management solutions to safeguard public health.

description: The project focuses on developing Aflasafe technology to combat aflatoxin contamination in key agricultural crops in Sierra Leone. The project aims to reduce aflatoxin levels, ensuring food safety and compliance with international standards for aflatoxin levels in crops such as maize and groundnuts. By utilizing biocontrol strategies the project addresses the critical issue of mycotoxin contamination, enhancing food quality and safety. The ultimate goal is to improve public health, increase access to global markets, and support sustainable agricultural practices in regions affected by aflatoxins.

description: A novel form of managed aquifer recharge known as underground transfer of floods for irrigation (UTFI) has been piloted in the Ganges Basin, enabling extensive evidence gathering and stakeholder engagment. UTFI has since been recognized as an important part of the solution to two crises facing India: destructive floods and recurring water shortages. The CGIAR Initiative on NEXUS Gains is now supporting the Government of Uttar Pradesh to better implement a national water conservation program. As a result, UTFI ponds and recharge wells have been constructed in hundreds more villages, increasing groundwater availability by up to 8 percent to date and strengthening climate resilience.

description: Through the implementation of the Enterprise Breeding System (EBS), multiple CGIAR and National Agricultural Research and Extension Systems (NARES) breeding teams adopted EBS as their central breeding data management platform. This initiative focused on harmonizing breeding operations across diverse centers and crop types. By integrating EBS into their workflows, these teams developed a disciplined approach to managing and utilizing data more efficiently. The adoption of EBS streamlined data collection, storage, and analysis, facilitating better decision-making, improving collaboration across centers, and enhancing the overall effectiveness of breeding programs. This alignment has strengthened the capacity of teams to conduct data-driven breeding operations, ultimately accelerating the development of improved crop varieties.

description: This innovation is a web-based data-driven tool that will help policy makers and implementers to manage, analyze, and report on groundwater data. This data will be crucial for making decisions about the long-term health of the state's groundwater resources. The tool will track factors like groundwater availability, quality, withdrawal, licensing, and more. This innovation is currently piloted in Punjab, Pakistan to support the Punjab Water Services Regulatory Authority, established under the Punjab Water Act 2019. It will be further upscaled to the country level in order to support implementation of National and provincial water policies.

description: The project developed a toolbox to understand the impact of gender norms on women’s economic reliance to climate change impacts. The adapted qualitative tools are used to identify and map the key stakeholders in agricultural and fisheries value chains and ii) understand which norms constrain women and other groups from participating in and benefiting from work in the different nodes of the value chain iii) how women and other value chain players at the different nodes of agricultural value chains are coping with climate change impacts and also make use of Vignettes and attitudes and behaviour assessment plots to analyze whether or not gender norms that may affect value chain actors are weakening or shifting. This analysis will also allow us to see under what conditions actors can deviate from the norm and how that impacts their economic resilience to climate change impacts.

description: More than 165 farmers in Nyando in Kenya have aggregated their land to form two large farms. One farm is 32 hectares in Agoro East sub-location aggregated by 83 farmers and the other in Jimo East sub-location we have a 10 hectare farm aggregated by 80 farmers. Farms will be design to embody permaculture principles in which farmers jointly designed various aspects of the farm including cereal reduction, vegetable production, fish ponds, irrigation, agro-forestry, apiculture and a section for livestock production. farmers jointly share resources, participate in joint production and value addition activities with the aim of achieving economies of scales while at the same time contributing to eco-system services and livelihoods. In Vihiga, where special aggregation is not possible, we have aggregated production at landscapes level with 52 farmers.

description: Banana production faces a serious threat from the invasive banana bunchy top virus (BBTV). Surveillance is challenging due to the fragmented nature of banana farming. We developed remote sensing-based Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to identify banana fields for targeted BBTV surveillance to address this. Using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data from the Copernicus Sentinel-1 satellite and AI algorithms such as random forest (RF) and convolutional neural networks (CNN), we achieved over 85% accuracy in identifying banana fields in Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and Ghana. We used Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) RGB images and the GoPro action camera photos to train and validate the models. These tools improve efficiency in mapping BBTV spread, aiding data-driven decisions for containment strategies and supporting sustainable banana production in African smallholder systems.

The Agroecological Living Landscape in the Transect of Kef Siliana has become a catalyst for positive change within rural communities and decision makers, focusing on increasing the cultivation, valorization, and use of forage crops and mixtures to enhance livestock feeding and restore Soil health. The enterprise has also strengthened its interactions with research institutions (INRAT, ICARDA) and has set up a tripartite agreement for the dissemination of adapted seeds and the application of agroecological practices on a larger scale.”

description: Yogurt Three Power is a functional yogurt with 3 high sources of protein and iron: spirulina, qushuro (Andean seaweed) and bovine blood. Probiotics will be added to these inputs, to later go through an encapsulation process. The already enriched capsules will be added to the yogurt, obtaining a product with high nutritional value. The encapsulation process will ensure correct assimilation by allowing the nutrients and probiotics to reach suitable areas of the digestive tract, thus differentiating them from existing dairy products. This product seeks to contribute to the fight against anemia in children in Peru.

description: The online Water Accounting Dashboard for the Souss Massa River Basin, Morocco, presents past, current, and potential future water status parameters such as water availability, water balance, and long-term changes in hydrology in an easily accessible, visual, and interactive manner for diverse stakeholders such as water management agencies, policy- and decision-makers. The Souss Massa River Basin has been hard hit by drought in recent years, resulting in reservoir water levels at historic lows. This innovation aims to bridge the communication divide between research findings and decision-makers to facilitate the informed, sustainable planning and management of scarce freshwater resources.

description: This innovation provides guidance for co-designing and implementing context-specific socio-technical innovation bundles (STIBs) that could contribute to women's empowerment and resilience through participatory processes like multi-stakeholder engagements.
